### V-253272 · WN11-00-000085 · CAT III: Standard local user accounts must not exist on a system in a domain.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253272r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Standard local user accounts must not exist on a system in a domain.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, use 'Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 35' for domain accounts. For local accounts, review 'Get-LocalUser' (LastLogon, PasswordExpires) and disable or delete accounts that aren't needed. Shared accounts require ISSO-documented justification.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Run "Computer Management".

Navigate to System Tools >> Local Users and Groups >> Users.

If local users other than the accounts listed below exist on a workstation in a domain, this is a finding.

The accounts listed assumes a system is joined to a domain and thus (per best practice), the local default accounts have been disabled.

For standalone or nondomain-joined systems, this is Not Applicable.

Built-in guest account (SID ending in 501)
Built-in DefaultAccount (SID ending in 503)
Built-in defaultuser0 (*SID unique per workstation)
Built-in WDAGUtilityAccount (SID ending in 504)
Local administrator account(s)

* Note: The SID for defaultuser0 is machine-specific and immutable (cannot be changed). It will differ per Windows installation.

Some of the built-in accounts may not exist on a system, depending on the Windows 11 version.
Refer to WN11-SO-000280 for requirement/guidance in use of Windows LAPS to manage the built-in administrator account password.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Limit local user accounts on domain-joined systems. Remove any unauthorized local accounts.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To minimize potential points of attack, local user accounts, other than built-in accounts and local administrator accounts, must not exist on a workstation in a domain. Users must log on to workstations in a domain with their domain accounts.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253273 · WN11-00-000090 · CAT II: Accounts must be configured to require password expiration.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253273r1268211_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000076-GPOS-00044 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse |
| CCI | CCI-004066, CCI-000199 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Accounts must be configured to require password expiration.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy: 'Maximum password age', 'Minimum password age', 'Enforce password history'. Domain values come from the Default Domain Policy or PSOs.

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Run "Computer Management".
Navigate to System Tools >> Local Users and Groups >> Users.
Double-click each active account.

If "Password never expires" is selected for any account, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure all passwords to expire.
Run "Computer Management".
Navigate to System Tools >> Local Users and Groups >> Users.
Double-click each active account.
Ensure "Password never expires" is not checked on all active accounts.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Passwords that do not expire increase exposure with a greater probability of being discovered or cracked.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000199**: The information system enforces maximum password lifetime restrictions.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (d)

### V-253274 · WN11-00-000095 · CAT II: Permissions for system files and directories must conform to minimum requirements.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253274r1016661_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00122 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-002165 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 (4) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 (4) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Permissions for system files and directories must conform to minimum requirements.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
The default file system permissions are adequate when the Security Option "Network access: Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users" is set to "Disabled" (WN11-SO-000160).

If the default file system permissions are maintained and the referenced option is set to "Disabled", this is not a finding.

Verify the default permissions for the sample directories below. Non-privileged groups such as Users or Authenticated Users must not have greater than read & execute permissions except where noted as defaults. (Individual accounts must not be used to assign permissions.)

Select the "Security" tab, and the "Advanced" button.

C:\
Type - "Allow" for all
Inherited from - "None" for all
Principal - Access - Applies to
Administrators - Full control - This folder, subfolders, and files
SYSTEM - Full control - This folder, subfolders, and files
Users - Read & execute - This folder, subfolders, and files
Authenticated Users - Modify - Subfolders and files only
Authenticated Users - Create folders / append data - This folder only

\Program Files

SYSTEM - Full control - Subfolders and files only

Administrators - Full control - Subfolders and files only
Users - Read & execute - This folder, subfolders, and files
CREATOR OWNER - Full control - Subfolders and files only
ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES - Read & execute - This folder, subfolders, and files
ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES - Read & execute - This folder, subfolders, and files

\Windows

Alternately use icacls.

Run "CMD" as administrator.
Enter "icacls" followed by the directory.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Maintain the default file system permissions and configure the Security Option: "Network access: Let everyone permissions apply to anonymous users" to "Disabled" (WN11-SO-000160).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Changing the system's file and directory permissions allows the possibility of unauthorized and anonymous modification to the operating system and installed applications.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002165**: Enforce organization-defined discretionary access control policies over defined subjects and objects.

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Internet Information System (IIS) or its subcomponents must not be installed on a workstation.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows Server, remove roles and features with 'Uninstall-WindowsFeature <Name>' or through Server Manager. On client OSes, use 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName <Name>'. Verify with 'Get-WindowsFeature | Where Installed' or 'Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online'.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify it has not been installed on the system.

Run "Programs and Features".
Select "Turn Windows features on or off".

If the entries for "Internet Information Services" or "Internet Information Services Hostable Web Core" are selected, this is a finding.

If an application requires IIS or a subset to be installed to function, this needs be documented with the ISSO. In addition, any applicable requirements from the IIS STIG must be addressed.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Uninstall "Internet Information Services" or "Internet Information Services Hostable Web Core" from the system.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** IIS is not installed by default. Installation of Internet Information System (IIS) may allow unauthorized internet services to be hosted. Websites must only be hosted on servers that have been designed for that purpose and can be adequately secured.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.

### V-268317 · WN11-00-000125 · CAT II: Copilot must be disabled for Windows 11.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-268317r1260009_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000096-GPOS-00050 |
| Topic | Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-000382 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Copilot must be disabled for this computer.

**Why it matters:** Modern computers like to "phone home", sending usage data to the manufacturer, syncing to personal cloud accounts, or showing ads and suggestions. This rule turns those features off or down so government information stays inside the government's systems, like not letting a delivery driver wander through the office and take notes.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PowerShell*: A powerful Windows command-line and scripting tool.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Users lose consumer conveniences such as Store apps, Microsoft-account sign-in and web results in search. Enterprise management may need a minimum telemetry level (e.g. for Windows Update for Business reports), so align the value with the STIG's allowed options.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Run the following PowerShell command as an administrator:

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers | Where-Object { $_.Name -like "*Copilot*" }

If Microsoft.Copilot displays, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Open PowerShell as an administrator. Run the following commands:

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers *CoPilot* | Remove-AppxPackage -AllUsers

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name "Microsoft.Windows.Ai.Copilot.Provider" | Remove-AppxPackage -AllUsers

Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object {$_.DisplayName -like "*Copilot*"} | Remove-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online

Note: Major Windows feature updates may reprovision default AppX packages. Running the PowerShell commands in a script as a post-update task or deploying it via a startup script is highly recommended for persistent environments.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Some features may communicate with the vendor, sending system information or downloading data or components for the feature. Turning off this capability will prevent potentially sensitive information from being sent outside the enterprise and uncontrolled updates to the system.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000382**: Configure the system to prohibit or restrict the use of organization-defined prohibited or restricted functions, system ports, protocols, software, and/or services.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 b · Rev 4: CM-7 b · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-279688 · WN11-00-000126 · CAT II: Windows 11 systems must block consumer account user authentication.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-279688r1256671_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must block consumer account user authentication.

**Why it matters:** Modern computers like to "phone home", sending usage data to the manufacturer, syncing to personal cloud accounts, or showing ads and suggestions. This rule turns those features off or down so government information stays inside the government's systems, like not letting a delivery driver wander through the office and take notes.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *Group Policy*: The central way Windows administrators push settings to many computers at once.
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\MicrosoftAccount | DisableUserAuth | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components | Microsoft Account "block all consumer Microsoft account user authentication | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Users lose consumer conveniences such as Store apps, Microsoft-account sign-in and web results in search. Enterprise management may need a minimum telemetry level (e.g. for Windows Update for Business reports), so align the value with the STIG's allowed options.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the "block all consumer Microsoft account user authentication" is enabled.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\MicrosoftAccount

Value Name: DisableUserAuth

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000001 (1)

If the registry value is not "1", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the following Group Policy:

Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Microsoft Account "block all consumer Microsoft account user authentication" to "Enabled".

For systems managed by Intune, apply the DoW Windows 11 STIG Settings Catalog (or equivalent Intune policy) found in the Intune policy package available on cyber.mil.

Steps to create an Intune policy:

1. Sign in to the Intune admin center >> Devices >> Configuration >> Create >> New Policy.
2. Platform: Windows 10 and later. Profile type: Settings Catalog, then click "Create".
3. Basics: Provide a Name and Description of the profile, then click "Next".
4. Configuration settings: Click "+ Add settings" and search for consumer under the Settings picker. Under the Administrative Templates\Windows Components\Microsoft account category, check the box next to "Block all consumer Microsoft account user authentication". Click the Enabled radio button, then click "Next".
5. Scope tags: (optional), then click "Next".
6. Assignments: Assign the policy to Entra security groups that contain the target users or devices, then click "Next".
7. Review + create: Review the deployment summary, then click "Create".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** It is detrimental for operating systems to provide, or install by default, functionality exceeding requirements or mission objectives. These unnecessary capabilities or services are often overlooked and therefore, may remain unsecured. They increase the risk to the platform by providing additional attack vectors.

Operating systems are capable of providing a wide variety of functions and services. Some of the functions and services, provided by default, may not be necessary to support essential organizational operations (e.g., key missions, functions).

The Copilot Rewrite functionality within Notepad and Image Generation within Paint is dependent upon the use of AI credits from a Microsoft 365 Personal or Family subscription. Organizational users must not use personal accounts to login to applications on enterprise machines.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Software certificate installation files must be removed from this computer.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Search all drives for *.p12 and *.pfx files.

If any files with these extensions exist, this is a finding.

This does not apply to server-based applications that have a requirement for .p12 certificate files (e.g., Oracle Wallet Manager) or Adobe PreFlight certificate files. Some applications create files with extensions of .p12 that are not certificate installation files. Removal of non-certificate installation files from systems is not required. These must be documented with the ISSO.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Remove any certificate installation files (*.p12 and *.pfx) found on a system.

Note: This does not apply to server-based applications that have a requirement for .p12 certificate files (e.g., Oracle Wallet Manager) or Adobe PreFlight certificate files.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Use of software certificates and their accompanying installation files for end users to access resources is less secure than the use of hardware-based certificates.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253281 · WN11-00-000135 · CAT II: A host-based firewall must be installed and enabled on the system.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253281r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Host Firewall |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** A host-based firewall must be installed and enabled on the system.

**Why it matters:** A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network connections are allowed in and out of the computer. This rule makes sure the gatekeeper is switched on and turns away anything that isn't on the approved list, like a security guard who only lets in people with an appointment.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Firewall*: A filter that decides which network connections are allowed in or out.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, use Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security. Turn it on for the Domain, Private and Public profiles with inbound set to block by default. Scope management rules (RDP, WinRM, SMB) to the management subnets. Verify with 'Get-NetFirewallProfile' and 'Get-NetFirewallRule'.

**Operational impact:** An over-restrictive default can cut off management or application traffic. Make changes from the console, or stage them with a timed rollback ('firewall-cmd --timeout').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Determine if a host-based firewall is installed and enabled on the system. If a host-based firewall is not installed and enabled on the system, this is a finding.

The configuration requirements will be determined by the applicable firewall STIG.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install and enable a host-based firewall on the system.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A firewall provides a line of defense against attack, allowing or blocking inbound and outbound connections based on a set of rules.

**Threat & control context:** A host firewall enforces deny-by-default, allow-by-exception at the endpoint (SC-7(5)) and contains lateral movement even when the perimeter is breached or the host sits on a flat network. Exposed ports must match the system's PPSM registration (CM-7(1)). Remote-management exceptions should be scoped to authorized management hosts rather than 'any'. Check that the firewall service can't be stopped by non-administrators and that rule changes are audited.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall; T1021 Remote Services; T1046 Network Service Discovery

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253282 · WN11-00-000140 · CAT II: Inbound exceptions to the firewall on Windows 11 domain workstations must only allow authorized remote management hosts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253282r991593_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00232 |
| Topic | Host Firewall, Remote Desktop & Remote Management |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Inbound exceptions to the firewall on this computer domain workstations must only allow authorized remote management hosts.

**Why it matters:** A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network connections are allowed in and out of the computer. This rule makes sure the gatekeeper is switched on and turns away anything that isn't on the approved list, like a security guard who only lets in people with an appointment.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *IP*: Internet Protocol: the addressing system that routes data between computers.
- *Firewall*: A filter that decides which network connections are allowed in or out.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security >> Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security | Inbound Rules (this link will be in the right pane) |  |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security. Turn it on for the Domain, Private and Public profiles with inbound set to block by default. Scope management rules (RDP, WinRM, SMB) to the management subnets. Verify with 'Get-NetFirewallProfile' and 'Get-NetFirewallRule'.

**Also related (Remote Desktop & Remote Management):** On Windows, RDP settings are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Remote Desktop Services >> Remote Desktop Session Host (Security / Device and Resource Redirection / Session Time Limits), and WinRM settings under Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM Client / WinRM Service). Verify WinRM with 'winrm get winrm/config'.

**Operational impact:** An over-restrictive default can cut off management or application traffic. Make changes from the console, or stage them with a timed rollback ('firewall-cmd --timeout').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify firewall exceptions to inbound connections on domain workstations include only authorized remote management hosts.

If allowed inbound exceptions are not limited to authorized remote management hosts, this is a finding.

Review inbound firewall exceptions.
Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security >> Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security >> Inbound Rules (this link will be in the right pane)

For any inbound rules that allow connections view the Scope for Remote IP address. This may be defined as an IP address, subnet, or range. The rule must apply to all firewall profiles.

If a third-party firewall is used, ensure comparable settings are in place.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure firewall exceptions to inbound connections on domain workstations to include only authorized remote management hosts.

Configure only inbound connection exceptions for authorized remote management hosts.
Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security >> Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security >> Inbound Rules (this link will be in the right pane)

For any inbound rules that allow connections, configure the Scope for Remote IP address to those of authorized remote management hosts. This may be defined as an IP address, subnet or range. Apply the rule to all firewall profiles.

If a third-party firewall is used, configure inbound exceptions to only include authorized remote management hosts.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Allowing inbound access to domain workstations from other systems may allow lateral movement across systems if credentials are compromised. Limiting inbound connections only from authorized remote management systems will help limit this exposure.

**Threat & control context:** A host firewall enforces deny-by-default, allow-by-exception at the endpoint (SC-7(5)) and contains lateral movement even when the perimeter is breached or the host sits on a flat network. Exposed ports must match the system's PPSM registration (CM-7(1)). Remote-management exceptions should be scoped to authorized management hosts rather than 'any'. Check that the firewall service can't be stopped by non-administrators and that rule changes are audited.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall; T1021 Remote Services; T1046 Network Service Discovery; T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253284 · WN11-00-000150 · CAT I: Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP) must be enabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253284r958928_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000433-GPOS-00192 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-002824 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-16 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-16 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP) must be enabled.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\kernel | DisableExceptionChainValidation | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide | Enable Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP) | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set these through Exploit Protection (system DEP, SEHOP, ASLR: 'Get-ProcessMitigation -System'), the 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security' policy under Device Guard, and the MS Security Guide 'Enable Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP)' policy.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify SEHOP is turned on.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\kernel\

Value Name: DisableExceptionChainValidation

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide >> "Enable Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP)" to "Enabled".

This policy setting requires the installation of the SecGuide custom templates included with the STIG package. "SecGuide.admx" and "SecGuide.adml" must be copied to the \Windows\PolicyDefinitions and \Windows\PolicyDefinitions\en-US directories respectively.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Attackers are constantly looking for vulnerabilities in systems and applications. Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP) blocks exploits that use the Structured Exception Handling overwrite technique, a common buffer overflow attack.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002824**: Implement organization-defined controls to protect the system memory from unauthorized code execution.  
  Rev 5: SI-16 · Rev 4: SI-16 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253285 · WN11-00-000155 · CAT II: The Windows PowerShell 2.0 feature must be disabled on the system.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253285r1153425_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software, PowerShell & Scripting Security |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Windows feature |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Windows PowerShell 2.0 feature must be disabled on the system.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PowerShell*: A powerful Windows command-line and scripting tool.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feature | Windows feature | MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root | Removed |

**How it works:** On Windows Server, remove roles and features with 'Uninstall-WindowsFeature <Name>' or through Server Manager. On client OSes, use 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName <Name>'. Verify with 'Get-WindowsFeature | Where Installed' or 'Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online'.

**Also related (PowerShell & Scripting Security):** On Windows, configure these under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Windows PowerShell: 'Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging' (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging EnableScriptBlockLogging = 1) and 'Turn on PowerShell Transcription'. Logs go to Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational. Write transcripts to a protected, centrally collected location.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
For Windows 11 version 24H2 and newer, this requirement is Not Applicable.

Run "Windows PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following:
Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online | Where FeatureName -like *PowerShellv2*

If either of the following have a "State" of "Enabled", this is a finding.

FeatureName : MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2
State : Enabled
FeatureName : MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root
State : Enabled

Alternately:
Search for "Features".

Select "Turn Windows features on or off".

If "Windows PowerShell 2.0" (whether the subcategory of "Windows PowerShell 2.0 Engine" is selected or not) is selected, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Disable "Windows PowerShell 2.0" on the system.

Run "Windows PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).
Enter the following:
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root

This command must disable both "MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root" and "MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2", which correspond to "Windows PowerShell 2.0" and "Windows PowerShell 2.0 Engine" respectively in "Turn Windows features on or off".

Alternately:
Search for "Features".
Select "Turn Windows features on or off".
De-select "Windows PowerShell 2.0".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Windows PowerShell 5.0 added advanced logging features, which can provide additional detail when malware has been run on a system. Disabling the Windows PowerShell 2.0 mitigates against a downgrade attack that evades the Windows PowerShell 5.0 script block logging feature.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter; T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell; T1059.005 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic; T1562.003 Impair Defenses: Impair Command History Logging

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253286 · WN11-00-000160 · CAT II: The Server Message Block (SMB) v1 protocol must be disabled on the system.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253286r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Windows feature |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Server Message Block (SMB) v1 protocol must be disabled on the system.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SMB*: Server Message Block: the protocol Windows uses for file and printer sharing.
- *PowerShell*: A powerful Windows command-line and scripting tool.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feature | Windows feature | SMB1Protocol | Removed |

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Different methods are available to disable SMBv1 on Windows 11. This is the preferred method, however if WN11-00-000165 and WN11-00-000170 are configured, this is NA.

Run "Windows PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following:
Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online | Where FeatureName -eq SMB1Protocol

If "State : Enabled" is returned, this is a finding.

Alternately:
Search for "Features".

Select "Turn Windows features on or off".

If "SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support" is selected, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Disable the SMBv1 protocol.

Run "Windows PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following:
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol

Alternately:
Search for "Features".

Select "Turn Windows features on or off".

De-select "SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** SMBv1 is a legacy protocol that uses the MD5 algorithm as part of SMB. MD5 is known to be vulnerable to a number of attacks such as collision and preimage attacks as well as not being FIPS compliant.

Disabling SMBv1 support may prevent access to file or print sharing resources with systems or devices that only support SMBv1. File shares and print services hosted on Windows Server 2003 are an example, however Windows Server 2003 is no longer a supported operating system. Some older Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices may only support SMBv1.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

---

SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253288 · WN11-00-000170 · CAT II: The Server Message Block (SMB) v1 protocol must be disabled on the SMB client.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253288r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Server Message Block (SMB) v1 protocol must be disabled on the SMB client.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *SMB*: Server Message Block: the protocol Windows uses for file and printer sharing.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\mrxsmb10 | Start | REG_DWORD = 0x00000004 (4) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide | Configure SMBv1 client driver | "Enabled" with "Disable driver (recommended)" selected for "Configure MrxSmb10 driver" |

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Different methods are available to disable SMBv1 on Windows 11, if WN11-00-000160is configured, this is NA.

If the following registry value is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\mrxsmb10\

Value Name: Start

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000004 (4)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide >> "Configure SMBv1 client driver" to "Enabled" with "Disable driver (recommended)" selected for "Configure MrxSmb10 driver".

This policy setting requires the installation of the SecGuide custom templates included with the STIG package. "SecGuide.admx" and "SecGuide.adml" must be copied to the \Windows\PolicyDefinitions and \Windows\PolicyDefinitions\en-US directories, respectively.

The system must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** SMBv1 is a legacy protocol that uses the MD5 algorithm as part of SMB. MD5 is known to be vulnerable to a number of attacks such as collision and preimage attacks as well as not being FIPS compliant.

Disabling SMBv1 support may prevent access to file or print sharing resources with systems or devices that only support SMBv1. File shares and print services hosted on Windows Server 2003 are an example, however Windows Server 2003 is no longer a supported operating system. Some older network attached devices may only support SMBv1.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253289 · WN11-00-000175 · CAT II: The Secondary Logon service must be disabled on Windows 11.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253289r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Secondary Logon service must be disabled on this computer.

**Why it matters:** Computers run many background programs ("services") all the time. This rule makes sure the important security ones are always running and the unneeded or risky ones are switched off, like keeping the alarm system armed while unplugging the appliances you don't use.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Before masking a service, confirm nothing depends on it ('systemctl list-dependencies --reverse <unit>').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Run "Services.msc".

Locate the "Secondary Logon" service.

If the "Startup Type" is not "Disabled" or the "Status" is "Running", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the "Secondary Logon" service "Startup Type" to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The Secondary Logon service provides a means for entering alternate credentials, typically used to run commands with elevated privileges. Using privileged credentials in a standard user session can expose those credentials to theft.

**Threat & control context:** Security functions such as auditd, firewalld, sshd's hardened configuration, fapolicyd and USBGuard only protect the system while their services are running. Conversely, every listening or socket-activated service is reachable attack surface. CM-7 (least functionality) and AU/SI controls require the security services to be enabled and the non-essential ones disabled or masked so they can't be started indirectly.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253290 · WN11-00-000190 · CAT II: Orphaned security identifiers (SIDs) must be removed from user rights on Windows 11.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253290r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management, Windows User Rights Assignment |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Orphaned security identifiers (SIDs) must be removed from user rights on this computer.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, use 'Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 35' for domain accounts. For local accounts, review 'Get-LocalUser' (LastLogon, PasswordExpires) and disable or delete accounts that aren't needed. Shared accounts require ISSO-documented justification.

**Also related (Windows User Rights Assignment):** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Review the effective User Rights setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

Review each User Right listed for any unresolved SIDs to determine whether they are valid, such as due to being temporarily disconnected from the domain. (Unresolved SIDs have the format of "*S-1-..".)

If any unresolved SIDs exist and are not for currently valid accounts or groups, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Remove any unresolved SIDs found in User Rights assignments and determined to not be for currently valid accounts or groups by removing the accounts or groups from the appropriate group policy.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Accounts or groups given rights on a system may show up as unresolved SIDs for various reasons including deletion of the accounts or groups. If the account or group objects are reanimated, there is a potential they may still have rights no longer intended. Valid domain accounts or groups may also show up as unresolved SIDs if a connection to the domain cannot be established for some reason.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation; T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253291 · WN11-00-000210 · CAT II: Bluetooth must be turned off unless approved by the organization.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253291r1259983_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Bluetooth must be turned off unless approved by the organization.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\PolicyManager\current\device\Connectivity | AllowBluetooth | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |

**How it works:** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This is NA if the system does not have Bluetooth.

Verify the Bluetooth radio is turned off unless approved by the organization. If it is not, this is a finding.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\PolicyManager\current\device\Connectivity\

Value Name: AllowBluetooth

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)

Approval for Bluetooth use must be documented with the information system security officer (ISSO).
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Turn off Bluetooth radios not organizationally approved.

For systems managed by Intune, apply the DoW Windows 11 STIG Settings Catalog (or equivalent Intune policy) found in the Intune policy package available on cyber.mil.
Steps to create an Intune policy:
1. Sign in to the Intune admin center >> Devices >> Configuration >> Create >> New Policy.
2. Platform: Windows 10 and later. Profile type: Settings Catalog, then click "Create".
3. Basics: Provide a Name and Description of the profile, then click "Next".
4. Configuration settings: Click "+ Add settings" and search for connectivity under the Settings picker. Under the Connectivity category, check the box next to "Allow Bluetooth setting". Choose the first option, "Disallow Bluetooth", then click "Next".
5. Scope tags: (optional), then click "Next".
6. Assignments: Assign the policy to Entra security groups that contain the target users or devices, then click "Next".
7. Review + create: Review the deployment summary, then click "Create".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If not configured properly, Bluetooth may allow rogue devices to communicate with a system. If a rogue device is paired with a system, there is potential for sensitive information to be compromised.

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253294 · WN11-00-000240 · CAT I: Administrative accounts must not be used with applications that access the internet, such as web browsers, or with potential internet sources, such as email.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253294r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Administrative accounts must not be used with applications that access the internet, such as web browsers, or with potential internet sources, such as email.

**Why it matters:** Modern computers like to "phone home", sending usage data to the manufacturer, syncing to personal cloud accounts, or showing ads and suggestions. This rule turns those features off or down so government information stays inside the government's systems, like not letting a delivery driver wander through the office and take notes.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Users lose consumer conveniences such as Store apps, Microsoft-account sign-in and web results in search. Enterprise management may need a minimum telemetry level (e.g. for Windows Update for Business reports), so align the value with the STIG's allowed options.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Determine whether administrative accounts are prevented from using applications that access the internet, such as web browsers, or with potential internet sources, such as email, except as necessary for local service administration.

The organization must have a policy that prohibits administrative accounts from using applications that access the internet, such as web browsers, or with potential internet sources, such as email, except as necessary for local service administration. The policy must define specific exceptions for local service administration. These exceptions may include HTTP(S)-based tools that are used for the administration of the local system, services, or attached devices.

Technical measures such as the removal of applications or application allowlisting must be used where feasible to prevent the use of applications that access the internet.

If accounts with administrative privileges are not prevented from using applications that access the internet or with potential internet sources, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Establish and enforce a policy that prohibits administrative accounts from using applications that access the internet, such as web browsers, or with potential internet sources, such as email. Define specific exceptions for local service administration. These exceptions may include HTTP(S)-based tools that are used for the administration of the local system, services, or attached devices.

Implement technical measures where feasible such as removal of applications or use of application allowlisting to restrict the use of applications that can access the internet.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Using applications that access the internet or have potential internet sources using administrative privileges exposes a system to compromise. If a flaw in an application is exploited while running as a privileged user, the entire system could be compromised. Web browsers and email are common attack vectors for introducing malicious code and must not be run with an administrative account.

Since administrative accounts may generally change or work around technical restrictions for running a web browser or other applications, it is essential that policy requires administrative accounts to not access the internet or use applications, such as email.

The policy must define specific exceptions for local service administration. These exceptions may include HTTP(S)-based tools that are used for the administration of the local system, services, or attached devices.

Technical means such as application allowlisting can be used to enforce the policy to ensure compliance.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b
