### V-253296 · WN11-00-000260 · CAT III: The Windows 11 time service must synchronize with an appropriate DoW time source.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253296r1256651_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000355-GPOS-00143 |
| Topic | Time Synchronization, Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-004923, CCI-001891 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-45 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-8 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's time service must synchronize with an appropriate DoW time source.

**Why it matters:** This keeps the computer's clock exactly in step with an official time source. That might sound minor, but security logs from different computers can only be pieced together if every clock agrees, and some sign-in systems refuse to work when clocks drift. It's like making sure all the witnesses' watches show the same time.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).
- *NTP / chrony*: Network Time Protocol: how computers keep their clocks accurate over the network.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Windows Time Service >> Time Providers | Configure Windows NTP Client | "Enabled", and configure the "NtpServer" field to point to an appropriate DoW time server |

**How it works:** On Windows, domain members sync from the domain hierarchy (NT5DS). The PDC emulator must point to an authoritative source using Administrative Templates >> System >> Windows Time Service >> Time Providers >> 'Configure Windows NTP Client'. Verify with 'w32tm /query /status'.

**Also related (Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features):** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Large clock corrections can confuse running applications. chrony slews gradually by default. Make sure the time servers are reachable through the firewall (UDP 123).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Review the Windows time service configuration.

Open an elevated "Command Prompt" (run as administrator).

Enter "W32tm /query /configuration".

Domain-joined systems (excluding the domain controller with the PDC emulator role):

If the value for "Type" under "NTP Client" is not "NT5DS", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the system to synchronize time with an appropriate DoW time source.

Domain-joined systems use NT5DS to synchronize time from other systems in the domain by default.

If the system needs to be configured to an NTP server, configure the system to point to an authorized time server by setting the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Windows Time Service >> Time Providers >> "Configure Windows NTP Client" to "Enabled", and configure the "NtpServer" field to point to an appropriate DoW time server.

The US Naval Observatory operates stratum 1 time servers, identified at https://www.cnmoc.usff.navy.mil/Our-Commands/United-States-Naval-Observatory/Precise-Time-Department/Network-Time-Protocol-NTP/. Time synchronization will occur through a hierarchy of time servers down to the local level. Clients and lower-level servers will synchronize with an authorized time server in the hierarchy.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The Windows Time Service controls time synchronization settings. Time synchronization is essential for authentication and auditing purposes. If the Windows Time Service is used, it must synchronize with a secure, authorized time source. Domain-joined systems are automatically configured to synchronize with domain controllers. If an NTP server is configured, it must synchronize with a secure, authorized time source.

**Threat & control context:** Accurate, synchronized time underpins log correlation across systems, Kerberos authentication (5-minute skew tolerance), certificate validity checks and forensic timelines (AU-8, AU-8(1) synchronization with an authoritative source, AU-8(2) secondary source). Time sources should be authenticated where possible and restricted to client mode, so the host can't be abused as an NTP amplifier.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.006 Indicator Removal: Timestomp; T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004923**: Compare the internal system clocks on an organization-defined frequency with organization-defined authoritative time source.  
  Rev 5: SC-45 (1) (a) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001891**: The information system compares internal information system clocks on an organization-defined frequency with an organization-defined authoritative time source.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: AU-8 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-257592 · WN11-00-000395 · CAT II: Windows 11 must not have portproxy enabled or in use.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-257592r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not have portproxy enabled or in use.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows Server, remove roles and features with 'Uninstall-WindowsFeature <Name>' or through Server Manager. On client OSes, use 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName <Name>'. Verify with 'Get-WindowsFeature | Where Installed' or 'Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online'.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Check the registry key for existence of proxied ports:
HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\PortProxy\.

If the key contains v4tov4\tcp\ or is populated v4tov4\tcp\, this is a finding.

Run "netsh interface portproxy show all".

If the command displays any results, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Contact the Administrator to run "netsh interface portproxy delete" with elevation. Remove any enabled portproxies that may be configured.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Having portproxy enabled or configured in Windows 10 could allow a man-in-the-middle attack.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-288475 · WN11-00-000400 · CAT II: All Wi-Fi Direct adapters must be disabled on the system.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-288475r1256669_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000096-GPOS-00050 |
| Topic | Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless |
| CCI | CCI-000382 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** All Wi-Fi Direct adapters must be disabled on the system.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PowerShell*: A powerful Windows command-line and scripting tool.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Determine whether any Wi-Fi Direct adapters exist on the system.

Open PowerShell with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following command:

Get-NetAdapter -InterfaceDescription "Microsoft Wi-Fi Direct*" -IncludeHidden

If there are no Wi-Fi Direct adapters configured on the system, no adapter information will display.

If any Wi-Fi Direct adapters are listed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Remove existing Wi-Fi Direct adapters from the system.

Open PowerShell with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following command:

Get-NetAdapter -InterfaceDescription "Microsoft Wi-Fi Direct*" -IncludeHidden | Disable-NetAdapter -Confirm:$false".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Wi-Fi Direct establishes a peer-to-peer (P2P) connection that lacks robust authentication. Due to its vulnerability to several types of attacks (including SSID spoofing and unauthorized network bridge), there is potential for sensitive information to be compromised.

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000382**: Configure the system to prohibit or restrict the use of organization-defined prohibited or restricted functions, system ports, protocols, software, and/or services.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 b · Rev 4: CM-7 b · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253297 · WN11-AC-000005 · CAT II: Windows 11 account lockout duration must be configured to 15 minutes or greater.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253297r958736_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128 |
| Topic | Account Lockout |
| CCI | CCI-002238 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's account lockout duration must be configured to 15 minutes or greater.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy | Account lockout duration | "15" minutes or greater |

**How it works:** Windows configures this under Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy (threshold, duration, reset counter). For domain accounts it is set in the Default Domain Policy or a Fine-Grained Password Policy, and local policy affects only local accounts.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy.

If the "Account lockout duration" is less than "15" minutes (excluding "0"), this is a finding.

Configuring this to "0", requiring an administrator to unlock the account, is more restrictive and is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy >> "Account lockout duration" to "15" minutes or greater.

A value of "0" is also acceptable, requiring an administrator to unlock the account.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The account lockout feature, when enabled, prevents brute-force password attacks on the system. This parameter specifies the amount of time that an account will remain locked after the specified number of failed logon attempts.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002238**: Automatically lock the account or node for either an organization-defined time period, until the locked account or node is released by an administrator, or delays the next logon prompt according to the organization-defined delay algorithm when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The number of allowed bad logon attempts must be configured to three or less.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy | Account lockout threshold | "3" or less invalid logon attempts (excluding "0" which is unacceptable) |

**How it works:** Windows configures this under Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy (threshold, duration, reset counter). For domain accounts it is set in the Default Domain Policy or a Fine-Grained Password Policy, and local policy affects only local accounts.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy.

If the "Account lockout threshold" is "0" or more than "3" attempts, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy >> "Account lockout threshold" to "3" or less invalid logon attempts (excluding "0" which is unacceptable).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The account lockout feature, when enabled, prevents brute-force password attacks on the system. The higher this value is, the less effective the account lockout feature will be in protecting the local system. The number of bad logon attempts must be reasonably small to minimize the possibility of a successful password attack, while allowing for honest errors made during a normal user logon.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a

### V-253300 · WN11-AC-000020 · CAT II: The password history must be configured to 24 passwords remembered.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253300r1256653_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000077-GPOS-00045 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse |
| CCI | CCI-004061 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (b) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The password history must be configured to 24 passwords remembered.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Group Policy*: The central way Windows administrators push settings to many computers at once.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy | Enforce password history | "24" passwords remembered |

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy: 'Maximum password age', 'Minimum password age', 'Enforce password history'. Domain values come from the Default Domain Policy or PSOs.

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

For GPO-managed systems, navigate to:

Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy.

Or

For Intune-managed systems, navigate to:

HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\PolicyManager\current\device\DeviceLock!DevicePasswordHistory

If the value for "Enforce password history" is less than "24" passwords remembered, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
For GPO-managed systems:

Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy >> "Enforce password history" to "24" passwords remembered.

For Intune-managed systems:

Revise the Intune policy to set password history policy to "24" passwords remembered.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A system is more vulnerable to unauthorized access when system users recycle the same password several times without being required to change a password to a unique password on a regularly scheduled basis. This enables users to effectively negate the purpose of mandating periodic password changes. The default value is 24 for Windows domain systems. DoW has determined this is the appropriate value for all Windows systems.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004061**: For password-based authentication, verify when users create or update passwords, that the passwords are not found on the list of commonly-used, expected, or compromised passwords in IA-5 (1) (a).  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (b) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Permitting passwords to be changed in immediate succession within the same day allows users to cycle passwords through their history database. This enables users to effectively negate the purpose of mandating periodic password changes.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000198**: The information system enforces minimum password lifetime restrictions.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (d)

### V-253303 · WN11-AC-000035 · CAT II: Passwords must, at a minimum, be 14 characters.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253303r1051044_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000078-GPOS-00046 |
| Topic | Password Strength & Complexity |
| CCI | CCI-004066, CCI-000205 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (a) |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Passwords must, at a minimum, be 14 characters.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy | Minimum password length | "14" characters |

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy ('Minimum password length', 'Password must meet complexity requirements'). Domain-wide values come from the Default Domain Policy or Fine-Grained Password Policies (PSOs). Lengths above 14 require the 'Relax minimum password length limits' setting on newer builds.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy.

If the value for the "Minimum password length," is less than "14" characters, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy >> "Minimum password length" to "14" characters.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Information systems not protected with strong password schemes (including passwords of minimum length) provide the opportunity for anyone to crack the password, thus gaining access to the system and compromising the device, information, or the local network.

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000205**: The information system enforces minimum password length.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (a) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (a)

| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (a) |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The built-in Microsoft password complexity filter must be enabled.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy | Password must meet complexity requirements | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy ('Minimum password length', 'Password must meet complexity requirements'). Domain-wide values come from the Default Domain Policy or Fine-Grained Password Policies (PSOs). Lengths above 14 require the 'Relax minimum password length limits' setting on newer builds.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy.

If the value for "Password must meet complexity requirements" is not set to "Enabled", this is a finding.

If the site is using a password filter that requires this setting be set to "Disabled" for the filter to be used, this would not be considered a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy >> "Password must meet complexity requirements" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The use of complex passwords increases their strength against guessing and brute-force attacks. This setting configures the system to verify that newly created passwords conform to the Windows password complexity policy.

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000192**: The information system enforces password complexity by the minimum number of upper case characters used.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (a) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (a)

### V-253305 · WN11-AC-000045 · CAT I: Reversible password encryption must be disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253305r1051046_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041 |
| Topic | Credential Storage & Password Hashing |
| CCI | CCI-004062, CCI-000196 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Reversible password encryption must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy | Store passwords using reversible encryption | "Disabled" |

**How it works:** Relevant Windows settings include 'Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' (NoLMHash), 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' (Disabled), and 'Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache' (CachedLogonsCount).

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy.

If the value for "Store password using reversible encryption" is not set to "Disabled", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy >> "Store passwords using reversible encryption" to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Storing passwords using reversible encryption is essentially the same as storing clear-text versions of the passwords. For this reason, this policy must never be enabled.

**Threat & control context:** When a host is compromised, stored credential material is the attacker's path to lateral movement. Weak or reversible storage (LM hashes, reversible encryption, low-iteration hashes, excessive cached domain logons) turns a single compromise into credential recovery for many accounts. IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004062**: For password-based authentication, store passwords using an approved salted key derivation function, preferably using a keyed hash.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000196**: The information system, for password-based authentication, stores only cryptographically-protected passwords.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (c) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (c)

### V-253306 · WN11-AU-000005 · CAT II: The system must be configured to audit Account Logon - Credential Validation failures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253306r991570_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000458-GPOS-00203 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The system must be configured to audit Account Logon - Credential Validation failures.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Account Logon | Audit Credential Validation | "Failure" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN11-SO-000030) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:
Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*".

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

Account Logon >> Credential Validation - Failure
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Account Logon >> "Audit Credential Validation" with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Credential validation records events related to validation tests on credentials for a user account logon.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

---

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The system must be configured to audit Account Management - User Account Management successes.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Account Management | Audit User Account Management | "Success" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN11-SO-000030) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:
Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*".

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

Account Management >> User Account Management - Success
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Account Management >> "Audit User Account Management" with "Success" selected.
```

### V-253313 · WN11-AU-000054 · CAT II: The system must be configured to audit Logon/Logoff - Account Lockout failures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253313r991578_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214 |
| Topic | Account Lockout, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The system must be configured to audit Logon/Logoff - Account Lockout failures.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Logon/Logoff | Audit Account Lockout | "Failure" selected |

**How it works:** Windows configures this under Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy (threshold, duration, reset counter). For domain accounts it is set in the Default Domain Policy or a Fine-Grained Password Policy, and local policy affects only local accounts.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN11-SO-000030) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:

Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").

Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*"

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

Logon/Logoff >> Account Lockout - Failure
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Logon/Logoff >> "Audit Account Lockout" with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Account Lockout events can be used to identify potentially malicious logon attempts.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Logon/Logoff | Audit Logon | "Failure" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN11-SO-000030) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:
Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*".

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

Logon/Logoff >> Logon - Failure
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Logon/Logoff >> "Audit Logon" with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Logon records user logons. If this is an interactive logon, it is recorded on the local system. If it is to a network share, it is recorded on the system accessed.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-253319 · WN11-AU-000081 · CAT II: Windows 11 must be configured to audit Object Access - File Share failures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253319r991572_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to audit Object Access - File Share failures.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access | Audit File Share | "Failure" selected |

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN11-SO-000030) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:

Open PowerShell or a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*"
Compare the AuditPol settings with the following:
Object Access >> File Share - Failure

If the system does not audit the above, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access >> "Audit File Share" with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Auditing file shares records events related to connection to shares on a system including system shares such as C$.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-253323 · WN11-AU-000085 · CAT II: The system must be configured to audit Object Access - Removable Storage failures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253323r991583_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000474-GPOS-00219 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing, Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The system must be configured to audit Object Access - Removable Storage failures.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access | Audit Removable Storage | "Failure" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Also related (Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless):** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN11-SO-000030) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:
Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*"

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

Object Access >> Removable Storage - Failure

Some virtual machines may generate excessive audit events for access to the virtual hard disk itself when this setting is enabled. This may be set to Not Configured in such cases and would not be a finding. This must be documented with the ISSO to include mitigations such as monitoring or restricting any actual removable storage connected to the VM.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access >> "Audit Removable Storage" with "Failure" selected.
```

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Privilege Use | Audit Sensitive Privilege Use | "Success" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN11-SO-000030) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:
Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*".

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

Privilege Use >> Sensitive Privilege Use - Success
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Privilege Use >> "Audit Sensitive Privilege Use" with "Success" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Sensitive Privilege Use records events related to use of sensitive privileges, such as "Act as part of the operating system" or "Debug programs".

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-253336 · WN11-AU-000160 · CAT II: The system must be configured to audit System - System Integrity successes.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253336r991573_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000463-GPOS-00207 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The system must be configured to audit System - System Integrity successes.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> System | Audit System Integrity | "Success" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN11-SO-000030) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:
Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*".

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

System >> System Integrity - Success
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> System >> "Audit System Integrity" with "Success" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

System Integrity records events related to violations of integrity to the security subsystem.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-253337 · WN11-AU-000500 · CAT II: The Application event log size must be configured to 32768 KB or greater.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253337r958752_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000341-GPOS-00132 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling |
| CCI | CCI-001849 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Application event log size must be configured to 32768 KB or greater.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\EventLog\Application | MaxSize | REG_DWORD = 0x00008000 (32768) (or greater) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Event Log Service >> Application | Specify the maximum log file size (KB) | "Enabled" with a "Maximum Log Size (KB)" of "32768" or greater |

**How it works:** On Windows, event log sizes are set under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Event Log Service >> Application/Security/System >> 'Specify the maximum log file size (KB)'. Forward events with Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) or a SIEM agent. Retention behavior is configured in the same policy node.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the system is configured to send audit records directly to an audit server, this is NA. This must be documented with the ISSO.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\EventLog\Application\

Value Name: MaxSize

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00008000 (32768) (or greater)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the system is configured to send audit records directly to an audit server, this is NA. This must be documented with the ISSO.

Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Event Log Service >> Application >> "Specify the maximum log file size (KB)" to "Enabled" with a "Maximum Log Size (KB)" of "32768" or greater.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inadequate log size will cause the log to fill up quickly. This may prevent audit events from being recorded properly and require frequent attention by administrative personnel.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001849**: Allocate audit log storage capacity to accommodate organization-defined audit log retention requirements.  
  Rev 5: AU-4 · Rev 4: AU-4 · Rev 3: n/a

If the system is configured to send audit records directly to an audit server, this requirement is not applicable. This must be documented with the information system security officer (ISSO).

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

NOTE: The following registry entry is an example; the value must equal at least one week's worth of records.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE

Value Type: REG_DWORD

```text

If the system is configured to send audit records directly to an audit server, this must be documented with the ISSO.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inadequate log size will cause the log to fill up quickly. **MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001849**: Allocate audit log storage capacity to accommodate organization-defined audit log retention requirements.
