### V-253340 · WN11-AU-000515 · CAT II: Windows 11 permissions for the Application event log must prevent access by non-privileged accounts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253340r958434_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000057-GPOS-00027 |
| Topic | Audit Log & Tool Protection, File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-000162 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-9 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-9 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's permissions for the Application event log must prevent access by non-privileged accounts.

**Why it matters:** The security diary is only useful if nobody can secretly edit or tear pages out of it. This rule locks down who can read or change the logs and the tools that manage them. It's like keeping the security camera footage in a locked room that only a couple of trusted people can enter.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, event log file permissions are on %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\*.evtx. The default ACL (Eventlog service, SYSTEM, Administrators) must not be broadened. The 'Manage auditing and security log' user right must be limited to Administrators.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the permissions on the Application event log (Application.evtx). Standard user accounts or groups must not have access. The default permissions listed below satisfy this requirement.

Eventlog - Full Control
SYSTEM - Full Control
Administrators - Full Control

The default location is the "%SystemRoot%\SYSTEM32\WINEVT\LOGS" directory. They may have been moved to another folder.

If the permissions for these files are not as restrictive as the ACLs listed, this is a finding.

Note: If "APPLICATION PACKAGE AUTHORITY\ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES" has Special Permissions, this would not be a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Ensure the permissions on the Application event log (Application.evtx) are configured to prevent standard user accounts or groups from having access. The default permissions listed below satisfy this requirement.

Eventlog - Full Control
SYSTEM - Full Control
Administrators - Full Control

The default location is the "%SystemRoot%\SYSTEM32\WINEVT\LOGS" directory.

If the location of the logs has been changed, when adding Eventlog to the permissions, it must be entered as "NT Service\Eventlog".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. The Application event log may be susceptible to tampering if proper permissions are not applied.

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000162**: Protect audit information from unauthorized access.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9

---

**How it works:** On Windows, event log file permissions are on %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\*.evtx. The default ACL (Eventlog service, SYSTEM, Administrators) must not be broadened. The 'Manage auditing and security log' user right must be limited to Administrators.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the permissions on the System event log (System.evtx). Standard user accounts or groups must not have access. The default permissions listed below satisfy this requirement.

Eventlog - Full Control
SYSTEM - Full Control
Administrators - Full Control

The default location is the "%SystemRoot%\SYSTEM32\WINEVT\LOGS" directory. They may have been moved to another folder.

If the permissions for these files are not as restrictive as the ACLs listed, this is a finding.

Note: If "APPLICATION PACKAGE AUTHORITY\ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES" has Special Permissions, this would not be a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Ensure the permissions on the System event log (System.evtx) are configured to prevent standard user accounts or groups from having access. The default permissions listed below satisfy this requirement.

Eventlog - Full Control
SYSTEM - Full Control
Administrators - Full Control

The default location is the "%SystemRoot%\SYSTEM32\WINEVT\LOGS" directory.

If the location of the logs has been changed, when adding Eventlog to the permissions, it must be entered as "NT Service\Eventlog".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. The System event log may be susceptible to tampering if proper permissions are not applied.

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000162**: Protect audit information from unauthorized access.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9

### V-253344 · WN11-AU-000555 · CAT II: Windows 11 must be configured to audit Other Policy Change Events Failures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253344r958412_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000130 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to audit Other Policy Change Events Failures.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Policy Change | Audit Other Policy Change Events | "Failure" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:
Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*".

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

Policy Change >> Other Policy Change Events - Failure
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Policy Change>> "Audit Other Policy Change Events" with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Audit Other Policy Change Events contains events about EFS Data Recovery Agent policy changes, changes in Windows Filtering Platform filter, status on Security policy settings updates for local Group Policy settings, Central Access Policy changes, and detailed troubleshooting events for Cryptographic Next Generation (CNG) operations.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3

### V-253347 · WN11-AU-000570 · CAT II: Windows 11 must be configured to audit Detailed File Share Failures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253347r958412_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000130 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to audit Detailed File Share Failures.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access | Audit Detailed File Share | "Failure" selected |

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Use the AuditPol tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:
Open a Command Prompt with elevated privileges ("Run as Administrator").
Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*".

Compare the AuditPol settings with the following. If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding:

Object Access >> Detailed File Share - Failure
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access >> Audit Detailed File Share" with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Audit Detailed File Share allows the user to audit attempts to access files and folders on a shared folder.
The Detailed File Share setting logs an event every time a file or folder is accessed, whereas the File Share setting only records one event for any connection established between a client and file share. Detailed File Share audit events include detailed information about the permissions or other criteria used to grant or deny access.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to audit handle manipulation failures.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access | Audit Handle Manipulation | "Failure" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that Audit Handle Manipulation auditing has been enabled:

Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access >> Audit Handle Manipulation.

If "Audit Handle Manipulation" is not set to "Failure", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access >> "Audit Handle Manipulation" with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior. Credential validation records events related to validation tests on credentials for a user account logon.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.

### V-253350 · WN11-CC-000005 · CAT II: Camera access from the lock screen must be disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253350r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless, Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Camera access from the lock screen must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Personalization | NoLockScreenCamera | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Control Panel >> Personalization | Prevent enabling lock screen camera | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Also related (Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout):** On Windows, set 'Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit' (InactivityTimeoutSecs <= 900) and 'Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior' (Lock Workstation). Personalization policies prevent the lock screen from showing slide shows or camera access.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the device does not have a camera, this is NA.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Personalization\

Value Name: NoLockScreenCamera

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the device does not have a camera, this is NA.

Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Control Panel >> Personalization >> "Prevent enabling lock screen camera" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enabling camera access from the lock screen could allow for unauthorized use. Requiring logon will ensure the device is only used by authorized personnel.

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

---

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On Windows, use Security Options such as 'Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in' and 'Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL' (Disabled). Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon covers enumerating local users, convenience PIN and picture password. Credential User Interface >> 'Do not display the password reveal button' handles the reveal button.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the device or operating system does not have a camera installed, this requirement is not applicable.

This requirement is not applicable to mobile devices (smartphones and tablets), where the use of the camera is a local authorizing official (AO) decision.

This requirement is not applicable to dedicated VTC suites located in approved VTC locations that are centrally managed.

For an external camera, if there is not a method for the operator to manually disconnect camera at the end of collaborative computing sessions, this is a finding.

For a built-in camera, the camera must be protected by a camera cover (e.g. laptop camera cover slide) when not in use. If the built-in camera is not protected with a camera cover, or if the built-in
camera is not disabled in the bios, this is a finding.

If the camera is not disconnected or covered, the following registry entry is required:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
RegistryPath\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\CapabilityAccessManager\ConsentStore\webcam

Value Name: Value                                                                             Value Data: Deny

If "Value Name" is set to a value other than "Deny" and the collaborative computing device has not been authorized for use, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the camera is not disconnected or covered, the following registry entry is required.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
RegistryPath\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\CapabilityAccessManager\ConsentStore\webcam

Value Name: Value                                                                            Value Data: Deny
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** It is detrimental for operating systems to provide, or install by default, functionality exceeding requirements or mission objectives. These unnecessary capabilities or services are often overlooked and therefore may remain unsecured. They increase the risk to the platform by providing additional attack vectors.

Failing to disconnect from collaborative computing devices (i.e. cameras) can result in subsequent compromises of organizational information. Providing easy methods to physically disconnect from such devices after a collaborative computing session helps to ensure that participants actually carry out the disconnect activity without having to go through complex and tedious procedures.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049, SRG-OS-000370-GPOS-00155

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions; T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253352 · WN11-CC-000010 · CAT II: The display of slide shows on the lock screen must be disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253352r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout, Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The display of slide shows on the lock screen must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Personalization | NoLockScreenSlideshow | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Control Panel >> Personalization | Prevent enabling lock screen slide show | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set 'Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit' (InactivityTimeoutSecs <= 900) and 'Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior' (Lock Workstation). Personalization policies prevent the lock screen from showing slide shows or camera access.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On Windows, use Security Options such as 'Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in' and 'Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL' (Disabled). Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon covers enumerating local users, convenience PIN and picture password. Credential User Interface >> 'Do not display the password reveal button' handles the reveal button.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Personalization\

Value Name: NoLockScreenSlideshow

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Control Panel >> Personalization >> "Prevent enabling lock screen slide show" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Slide shows that are displayed on the lock screen could display sensitive information to unauthorized personnel. Turning off this feature will limit access to the information to a logged on user.

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1087 Account Discovery

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253353 · WN11-CC-000020 · CAT II: IPv6 source routing must be configured to highest protection.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253353r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** IPv6 source routing must be configured to highest protection.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *IP*: Internet Protocol: the addressing system that routes data between computers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters | DisableIpSourceRouting | REG_DWORD = 2 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MSS (Legacy) | MSS: (DisableIPSourceRouting IPv6) IP source routing protection level (protects against packet spoofing) | "Highest protection, source routing is completely disabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set these through MSS (Legacy) templates included with the STIG GPO package (DisableIPSourceRouting, EnableICMPRedirect, NoNameReleaseOnDemand) and Network >> DNS Client >> 'Turn off multicast name resolution' (EnableMulticast = 0). Hardened UNC Paths requires mutual authentication and integrity for \\*\SYSVOL and \\*\NETLOGON.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters\

Value Name: DisableIpSourceRouting

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 2
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MSS (Legacy) >> "MSS: (DisableIPSourceRouting IPv6) IP source routing protection level (protects against packet spoofing)" to "Highest protection, source routing is completely disabled".

This policy setting requires the installation of the MSS-Legacy custom templates included with the STIG package. "MSS-Legacy.admx" and "MSS-Legacy.adml" must be copied to the \Windows\PolicyDefinitions and \Windows\PolicyDefinitions\en-US directories respectively.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Configuring the system to disable IPv6 source routing protects against spoofing.

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

---

### V-253357 · WN11-CC-000037 · CAT II: Local administrator accounts must have their privileged token filtered to prevent elevated privileges from being used over the network on domain systems.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253357r958518_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000134-GPOS-00068 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication, Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-001084 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Local administrator accounts must have their privileged token filtered to prevent elevated privileges from being used over the network on domain systems.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *UAC*: User Account Control: the Windows pop-up that asks for confirmation before something makes system-wide changes.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System | LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide | Apply UAC restrictions to local accounts on network logons | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Also related (Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening):** On Windows these are Security Options ('Accounts: Rename administrator account', 'Accounts: Guest account status', 'Accounts: Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only') plus LAPS for unique, rotated local administrator passwords.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the system is not a member of a domain, this is NA.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\

Value Name: LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide >> "Apply UAC restrictions to local accounts on network logons" to "Enabled".

This policy setting requires the installation of the SecGuide custom templates included with the STIG package. "SecGuide.admx" and "SecGuide.adml" must be copied to the \Windows\PolicyDefinitions and \Windows\PolicyDefinitions\en-US directories respectively.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A compromised local administrator account can provide means for an attacker to move laterally between domain systems.

With User Account Control enabled, filtering the privileged token for built-in administrator accounts will prevent the elevated privileges of these accounts from being used over the network.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process; T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001084**: Isolate security functions from nonsecurity functions.  
  Rev 5: SC-3 · Rev 4: SC-3 · Rev 3: SC-3

### V-253358 · WN11-CC-000038 · CAT II: WDigest Authentication must be disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253358r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Windows Authentication Protocols (NTLM, Kerberos, LSA), Remote Desktop & Remote Management |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** WDigest Authentication must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** When you log into a Windows network, your computer and the server trade secret "handshakes" to prove who you are. Older handshakes are easy for attackers to fake or steal. This rule switches off the old, weak handshakes and protects the part of memory where Windows keeps your sign-in secrets, like retiring an old ID badge design that was easy to forge.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\Wdigest | UseLogonCredential | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide | WDigest Authentication (disabling may require KB2871997) | "Disabled" |

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). Key settings include 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' (LmCompatibilityLevel = 5), 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos', 'Minimum session security for NTLM SSP', WDigest 'UseLogonCredential' = 0, and Credential Guard via Device Guard >> 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security'. Verify with 'gpresult /h' or the registry paths shown in the check.

**Also related (Remote Desktop & Remote Management):** On Windows, RDP settings are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Remote Desktop Services >> Remote Desktop Session Host (Security / Device and Resource Redirection / Session Time Limits), and WinRM settings under Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM Client / WinRM Service). Verify WinRM with 'winrm get winrm/config'.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\Wdigest\

Value Name: UseLogonCredential

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide >> "WDigest Authentication (disabling may require KB2871997)" to "Disabled".

The patch referenced in the policy title is not required for Windows 11.

This policy setting requires the installation of the SecGuide custom templates included with the STIG package. "SecGuide.admx" and "SecGuide.adml" must be copied to the \Windows\PolicyDefinitions and \Windows\PolicyDefinitions\en-US directories respectively.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** When the WDigest Authentication protocol is enabled, plain text passwords are stored in the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) exposing them to theft. WDigest is disabled by default in Windows 11. This setting ensures this is enforced.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253359 · WN11-CC-000039 · CAT II: Run as different user must be removed from context menus.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253359r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo) |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Run as different user must be removed from context menus.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE | SuppressionPolicy | REG_DWORD = 0x00001000 (4096) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide | Remove "Run as Different User" from context menus | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** UAC settings are Security Options named 'User Account Control: ...' (registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System: EnableLUA, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin, ConsentPromptBehaviorUser, FilterAdministratorToken, EnableInstallerDetection, EnableSecureUIAPaths, EnableVirtualization).

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry values do not exist or are not configured as specified, this is a finding.
The policy configures the same Value Name, Type and Value under four different registry paths.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Paths:
\SOFTWARE\Classes\batfile\shell\runasuser\
\SOFTWARE\Classes\cmdfile\shell\runasuser\
\SOFTWARE\Classes\exefile\shell\runasuser\
\SOFTWARE\Classes\mscfile\shell\runasuser\

Value Name: SuppressionPolicy

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00001000 (4096)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide >> "Remove "Run as Different User" from context menus" to "Enabled".

This policy setting requires the installation of the SecGuide custom templates included with the STIG package. "SecGuide.admx" and "SecGuide.adml" must be copied to the \Windows\PolicyDefinitions and \Windows\PolicyDefinitions\en-US directories respectively.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "Run as different user" selection from context menus allows the use of credentials other than the currently logged on user. Using privileged credentials in a standard user session can expose those credentials to theft. Removing this option from context menus helps prevent this from occurring.

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253360 · WN11-CC-000040 · CAT II: Insecure logons to an SMB server must be disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253360r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access, Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Insecure logons to an SMB server must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SMB*: Server Message Block: the protocol Windows uses for file and printer sharing.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\LanmanWorkstation | AllowInsecureGuestAuth | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Network >> Lanman Workstation | Enable insecure guest logons | "Disabled" |

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Also related (Network Stack Hardening):** On Windows, set these through MSS (Legacy) templates included with the STIG GPO package (DisableIPSourceRouting, EnableICMPRedirect, NoNameReleaseOnDemand) and Network >> DNS Client >> 'Turn off multicast name resolution' (EnableMulticast = 0). Hardened UNC Paths requires mutual authentication and integrity for \\*\SYSVOL and \\*\NETLOGON.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\LanmanWorkstation\

Value Name: AllowInsecureGuestAuth

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Network >> Lanman Workstation >> "Enable insecure guest logons" to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Insecure guest logons allow unauthenticated access to shared folders. Shared resources on a system must require authentication to establish proper access.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253361 · WN11-CC-000044 · CAT II: Internet connection sharing must be disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253361r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Internet connection sharing must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Network Connections | NC_ShowSharedAccessUI | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Network >> Network Connections | Prohibit use of Internet Connection Sharing on your DNS domain network | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set these through MSS (Legacy) templates included with the STIG GPO package (DisableIPSourceRouting, EnableICMPRedirect, NoNameReleaseOnDemand) and Network >> DNS Client >> 'Turn off multicast name resolution' (EnableMulticast = 0). Hardened UNC Paths requires mutual authentication and integrity for \\*\SYSVOL and \\*\NETLOGON.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Network Connections\

Value Name: NC_ShowSharedAccessUI

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Network >> Network Connections >> "Prohibit use of Internet Connection Sharing on your DNS domain network" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Internet connection sharing makes it possible for an existing internet connection, such as through wireless, to be shared and used by other systems essentially creating a mobile hotspot. This exposes the system sharing the connection to others with potentially malicious purpose.

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

|---|---|---|---|

SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

Hardened UNC Paths requires mutual authentication and integrity for \\*\SYSVOL and \\*\NETLOGON.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This requirement is applicable to domain-joined systems, for standalone systems this is NA.

If the following registry values do not exist or are not configured as specified, this is a finding.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\NetworkProvider\HardenedPaths\

Value Name: \\*\NETLOGON

Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

### V-253363 · WN11-CC-000052 · CAT II: Windows 11 must be configured to prioritize ECC Curves with longer key lengths first.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253363r1268232_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000120-GPOS-00061 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140) |
| CCI | CCI-000803 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to prioritize ECC Curves with longer key lengths first.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Cryptography\Configuration\SSL\00010002 | EccCurves | REG_MULTI_SZ = NistP384 NistP256 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Network >> SSL Configuration Settings | ECC Curve Order | Only: NistP384, NistP256 |

**How it works:** On Windows, 'System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing' (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\FIPSAlgorithmPolicy\Enabled) restricts Schannel and CNG to FIPS-approved algorithms. Related settings cover Kerberos encryption types and NTLM session security.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java and .NET code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Cryptography\Configuration\SSL\00010002\

Value Name: EccCurves

Value Type: REG_MULTI_SZ
Value: NistP384 NistP256
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Network >> SSL Configuration Settings >> "ECC Curve Order" to "Enabled" with "ECC Curve Order:" including the following in the order listed:

NistP384
NistP256
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Use of weak or untested encryption algorithms undermines the purposes of utilizing encryption to protect data. By default Windows uses ECC curves with shorter key lengths first. Requiring ECC curves with longer key lengths to be prioritized first helps ensure more secure algorithms are used.

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000803**: Implement mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module that meet the requirements of applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance for such authentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-7 · Rev 4: IA-7 · Rev 3: IA-7

### V-253364 · WN11-CC-000055 · CAT II: Simultaneous connections to the internet or a Windows domain must be limited.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253364r1268254_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000481-GPOS-00481 |
| Topic | Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-002418 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Simultaneous connections to the internet or a Windows domain must be limited.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WcmSvc\GroupPolicy | fMinimizeConnections | REG_DWORD = 3 (or if the Value Name does not exist) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Network >> Windows Connection Manager | Minimize the number of simultaneous connections to the Internet or a Windows Domain | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set these through MSS (Legacy) templates included with the STIG GPO package (DisableIPSourceRouting, EnableICMPRedirect, NoNameReleaseOnDemand) and Network >> DNS Client >> 'Turn off multicast name resolution' (EnableMulticast = 0). Hardened UNC Paths requires mutual authentication and integrity for \\*\SYSVOL and \\*\NETLOGON.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
The default behavior for "Minimize the number of simultaneous connections to the Internet or a Windows Domain" is "Enabled".

If it exists and is configured with a value of "0", this is a finding.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WcmSvc\GroupPolicy\

Value Name: fMinimizeConnections

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 3 (or if the Value Name does not exist)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
The default behavior for "Minimize the number of simultaneous connections to the Internet or a Windows Domain" is "Enabled".

If this needs to be corrected, configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Network >> Windows Connection Manager >> "Minimize the number of simultaneous connections to the Internet or a Windows Domain" to "Enabled".  Under "Options", set "Minimize Policy Options" to "3 = Prevent Wi-Fi When on Ethernet".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Multiple network connections can provide additional attack vectors to a system and must be limited. The "Minimize the number of simultaneous connections to the Internet or a Windows Domain" setting prevents systems from automatically establishing multiple connections. When both wired and wireless connections are available, for example, the less preferred connection (typically wireless) will be disconnected.

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002418**: Protect the confidentiality and/or integrity of transmitted information.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 · Rev 4: SC-8 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-268318 · WN11-CC-000063 · CAT II: Windows 11 systems must use either Group Policy or an approved Mobile Device Management (MDM) product to enforce STIG compliance.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-268318r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must use either Group Policy or an approved Mobile Device Management (MDM) product to enforce STIG compliance.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *Group Policy*: The central way Windows administrators push settings to many computers at once.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows Server, remove roles and features with 'Uninstall-WindowsFeature <Name>' or through Server Manager. On client OSes, use 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName <Name>'. Verify with 'Get-WindowsFeature | Where Installed' or 'Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online'.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Windows 11 system is receiving policy from either group Policy or an MDM with the following steps:

From a command line or PowerShell:

gpresult /R
OS Configuration: Member Workstation

If the system OS Configuration is set to "Member Workstation", the system is being managed by GPO.

If the system OS Configuration is set to "Standalone Workstation" and is not being managed by GPO, ask the administrator to indicate which MDM is managing the device.

Issue to the following for Intune. Note: Intune must be running at time of command.

From PowerShell: Get-Service -Name "IntuneManagementExtension"

This should return the following result:

Status = Running, Name = IntuneManagementExtension, DisplayName = Microsoft Intune Management Extension

If Intune is not installed, the response will include "ObjectNotFound" and/or "NoServiceFoundForGivenName".

If the Windows 11 system is not receiving policy from either group Policy or an MDM (that is running), this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Windows 11 system to use either Group Policy or an approved MDM product to enforce STIG compliance.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without Windows 11 systems being managed, devices could be rogue and become targets of an attacker.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b
