### V-253367 · WN11-CC-000066 · CAT II: Command line data must be included in process creation events.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253367r958422_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000135 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3 (1) |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Command line data must be included in process creation events.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit | ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Audit Process Creation | Include command line in process creation events | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit\

Value Name: ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Audit Process Creation >> "Include command line in process creation events" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Enabling "Include command line data for process creation events" will record the command line information with the process creation events in the log. This can provide additional detail when malware has run on a system.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)

### V-253368 · WN11-CC-000068 · CAT II: Windows 11 must be configured to enable Remote host allows delegation of non-exportable credentials.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253368r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Windows Authentication Protocols (NTLM, Kerberos, LSA) |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to enable Remote host allows delegation of non-exportable credentials.

**Why it matters:** When you log into a Windows network, your computer and the server trade secret "handshakes" to prove who you are. Older handshakes are easy for attackers to fake or steal. This rule switches off the old, weak handshakes and protects the part of memory where Windows keeps your sign-in secrets, like retiring an old ID badge design that was easy to forge.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CredentialsDelegation | AllowProtectedCreds | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Credentials Delegation | Remote host allows delegation of non-exportable credentials | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). Key settings include 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' (LmCompatibilityLevel = 5), 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos', 'Minimum session security for NTLM SSP', WDigest 'UseLogonCredential' = 0, and Credential Guard via Device Guard >> 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security'. Verify with 'gpresult /h' or the registry paths shown in the check.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CredentialsDelegation\

Value Name: AllowProtectedCreds

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000001 (1)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Credentials Delegation >> "Remote host allows delegation of non-exportable credentials" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** An exportable version of credentials is provided to remote hosts when using credential delegation which exposes them to theft on the remote host. Restricted Admin mode or Remote Credential Guard allow delegation of non-exportable credentials providing additional protection of the credentials. Enabling this configures the host to support Restricted Admin mode or Remote Credential Guard.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253369 · WN11-CC-000070 · CAT II: Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) must be enabled on Windows 11 with the platform security level configured to Secure Boot or Secure Boot with DMA Protection.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253369r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations, Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) must be enabled on this computer with the platform security level configured to Secure Boot or Secure Boot with DMA Protection.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *UEFI / Secure Boot*: Modern computer firmware and its feature that only lets trusted software start the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard | EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard | RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures | REG_DWORD = 1 (Secure Boot only) or 3 (Secure Boot and DMA Protection) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Device Guard | Turn On virtualization-based Security | "Enabled" with "Secure Boot" or "Secure Boot and DMA Protection" selected for "Select Platform Security Level:" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set these through Exploit Protection (system DEP, SEHOP, ASLR: 'Get-ProcessMitigation -System'), the 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security' policy under Device Guard, and the MS Security Guide 'Enable Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP)' policy.

**Also related (Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless):** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Confirm VBS is enabled and running with Secure Boot or Secure Boot and DMA Protection.

If there are documented operational mission needs to disable VBS, this may be reduced to a CAT III finding.

Run "PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following:

"Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard"

If "RequiredSecurityProperties" does not include a value of "2" indicating "Secure Boot" (e.g., "{1, 2}"), this is a finding.

If "Secure Boot and DMA Protection" is configured, "3" will also be displayed in the results (e.g., "{1, 2, 3}").

If "VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus" is not a value of "2" indicating "Running", this is a finding.

Alternately:

Run "System Information".

Under "System Summary", verify the following:

If "Device Guard virtualization-based security" does not display "Running", this is a finding.

If "Device Guard Required Security Properties" does not display "Base Virtualization Support, Secure Boot", this is a finding.

If "Secure Boot and DMA Protection" is configured, "DMA Protection" will also be displayed (e.g., "Base Virtualization Support, Secure Boot, DMA Protection").

The policy settings referenced in the Fix section will configure the following registry values. However, due to hardware requirements, the registry values alone do not ensure proper function.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard\

Value Name: EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity
Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1

Value Name: RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures
Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1 (Secure Boot only) or 3 (Secure Boot and DMA Protection)

A Microsoft article on the Credential Guard system requirement can be found at the following link:

https://technet.microsoft.com/en-us/itpro/windows/keep-secure/credential-guard-requirements
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Device Guard >> "Turn On virtualization-based Security" to "Enabled" with "Secure Boot" or "Secure Boot and DMA Protection" selected for "Select Platform Security Level:".

A Microsoft article on Credential Guard system requirement can be found at the following link.
https://technet.microsoft.com/en-us/itpro/windows/keep-secure/credential-guard-requirements
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** VBS provides the platform for the additional security features, Credential Guard, and virtualization-based protection of code integrity. Secure Boot is the minimum security level, with DMA protection providing additional memory protection. DMA Protection requires a CPU that supports input/output memory management unit (IOMMU).

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution; T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

**In plain terms:** Credential Guard must be running on this computer.

This rule switches off the old, weak handshakes and protects the part of memory where Windows keeps your sign-in secrets, like retiring an old ID badge design that was easy to forge.

|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard | LsaCfgFlags | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) (Enabled with UEFI lock) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Device Guard | Turn On virtualization-based Security | "Enabled" with "Enabled with UEFI lock" selected for "Credential Guard Configuration:" |

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). Key settings include 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' (LmCompatibilityLevel = 5), 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos', 'Minimum session security for NTLM SSP', WDigest 'UseLogonCredential' = 0, and Credential Guard via Device Guard >> 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security'. Verify with 'gpresult /h' or the registry paths shown in the check.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Confirm Credential Guard is running.

Run "PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following:

"Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard"

If "SecurityServicesRunning" does not include a value of "1" (e.g., "{1, 2}"), this is a finding.

Alternately:

Run "System Information".

Under "System Summary", verify the following:

If "virtualization-based Services Running" does not list "Credential Guard", this is a finding.

The policy settings referenced in the Fix section will configure the following registry value. However, due to hardware requirements, the registry value alone does not ensure proper function.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard\

Value Name: LsaCfgFlags
Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000001 (1) (Enabled with UEFI lock)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Device Guard >> "Turn On virtualization-based Security" to "Enabled" with "Enabled with UEFI lock" selected for "Credential Guard Configuration:".

A Microsoft TechNet article on Credential Guard, including system requirement details, can be found at the following link:

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/access-protection/credential-guard/credential-guard
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to protect information that could be used in credential theft attacks if compromised. This authentication information, which was stored in the Local Security Authority (LSA) in previous versions of Windows, is isolated from the rest of operating system and can only be accessed by privileged system software.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253371 · WN11-CC-000080 · CAT II: Virtualization-based protection of code integrity must be enabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253371r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations, Mandatory Access & Application Control |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Virtualization-based protection of code integrity must be enabled.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *UEFI / Secure Boot*: Modern computer firmware and its feature that only lets trusted software start the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard | HypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) (Enabled with UEFI lock), or 0x00000002 (2) (Enabled without lock) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Device Guard | Turn On virtualization-based Security | "Enabled" with "Enabled with UEFI lock" or "Enabled without lock" selected for "virtualization-based Protection of Code Integrity:" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set these through Exploit Protection (system DEP, SEHOP, ASLR: 'Get-ProcessMitigation -System'), the 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security' policy under Device Guard, and the MS Security Guide 'Enable Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP)' policy.

**Also related (Mandatory Access & Application Control):** On Windows, AppLocker policies are under Security Settings >> Application Control Policies, which requires the Application Identity service. WDAC policies are deployed through Intune, ConfigMgr or GPO. Run in audit mode first and review the event logs.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Confirm virtualization-based protection of code integrity.

If there are documented operational mission needs to disable code integrity, this may be reduced to a CAT II finding.

Run "PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following:

"Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard"

If "SecurityServicesRunning" does not include a value of "2" (e.g., "{1, 2}"), this is a finding.

Alternately:

Run "System Information".

Under "System Summary", verify the following:

If "Virtualization-based Security Services Running" does not list "Hypervisor enforced Code Integrity", this is a finding.

The policy settings referenced in the Fix section will configure the following registry value. However, due to hardware requirements, the registry value alone does not ensure proper function.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard\

Value Name: HypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity
Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000001 (1) (Enabled with UEFI lock), or 0x00000002 (2) (Enabled without lock)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Device Guard >> "Turn On virtualization-based Security" to "Enabled" with "Enabled with UEFI lock" or "Enabled without lock" selected for "virtualization-based Protection of Code Integrity:".

"Enabled with UEFI lock" is preferred as more secure; however, it cannot be turned off remotely through a group policy change if there is an issue.

"Enabled without lock" will allow this to be turned off remotely while testing for issues.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Virtualization-based protection of code integrity enforces kernel mode memory protections as well as protecting Code Integrity validation paths. This isolates the processes from the rest of the operating system and can only be accessed by privileged system software.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution; T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253372 · WN11-CC-000085 · CAT II: Early Launch Antimalware, Boot-Start Driver Initialization Policy must prevent boot drivers.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253372r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations, Anti-Malware & Reputation Protection |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Early Launch Antimalware, Boot-Start Driver Initialization Policy must prevent boot drivers.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\EarlyLaunch | DriverLoadPolicy | REG_DWORD = 1, 3, or 8 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Early Launch Antimalware | Boot-Start Driver Initialization Policy | "Enabled with "Good, unknown and bad but critical" selected |

**How it works:** On Windows, set these through Exploit Protection (system DEP, SEHOP, ASLR: 'Get-ProcessMitigation -System'), the 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security' policy under Device Guard, and the MS Security Guide 'Enable Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection (SEHOP)' policy.

**Also related (Anti-Malware & Reputation Protection):** On Windows, configure Microsoft Defender Antivirus under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Microsoft Defender Antivirus, and SmartScreen under Windows Components >> File Explorer and Microsoft Edge. Verify with 'Get-MpComputerStatus' (AMServiceEnabled, AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated). If a third-party DoD-approved product is deployed, Defender may run in passive mode.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
The default behavior is for Early Launch Antimalware - Boot-Start Driver Initialization policy is to enforce "Good, unknown and bad but critical" (preventing "bad").

If the registry value name below does not exist, this is a finding.

If it exists and is configured with a value of "7", this is a finding.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\EarlyLaunch\

Value Name: DriverLoadPolicy

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1, 3, or 8

Possible values for this setting are:
8 - Good only
1 - Good and unknown
3 - Good, unknown and bad but critical
7 - All (which includes "Bad" and would be a finding)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Ensure that Early Launch Antimalware - Boot-Start Driver Initialization policy is set to enforce "Good, unknown and bad but critical" (preventing "bad").

To correct this, configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Early Launch Antimalware >> "Boot-Start Driver Initialization Policy" to "Enabled with "Good, unknown and bad but critical" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The default behavior is for Early Launch Antimalware - Boot-Start Driver Initialization policy is to enforce "Good, unknown and bad but critical" (preventing "bad"). By being launched first by the kernel, ELAM ( Early Launch Antimalware) is ensured to be launched before any third-party software, and is therefore able to detect malware in the boot process and prevent it from initializing.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution; T1562.001 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools; T1204 User Execution; T1566 Phishing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253373 · WN11-CC-000090 · CAT II: Group Policy objects must be reprocessed even if they have not changed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253373r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Active Directory & Domain Controller Security |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Group Policy objects must be reprocessed even if they have not changed.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Group Policy*: The central way Windows administrators push settings to many computers at once.
- *Registry*: Windows' internal database of settings.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Group Policy\{35378EAC-683F-11D2-A89A-00C04FBBCFA2} | NoGPOListChanges | REG_DWORD = 0 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Group Policy | Configure registry policy processing | "Enabled" and select the option "Process even if the Group Policy objects have not changed" |

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Group Policy\{35378EAC-683F-11D2-A89A-00C04FBBCFA2}

Value Name: NoGPOListChanges

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Group Policy >> "Configure registry policy processing" to "Enabled" and select the option "Process even if the Group Policy objects have not changed".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enabling this setting and then selecting the "Process even if the Group Policy objects have not changed" option ensures that the policies will be reprocessed even if none have been changed. This way, any unauthorized changes are forced to match the domain-based group policy settings again.

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253374 · WN11-CC-000100 · CAT II: Downloading print driver packages over HTTP must be prevented.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253374r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Downloading print driver packages over HTTP must be prevented.

**Why it matters:** Modern computers like to "phone home", sending usage data to the manufacturer, syncing to personal cloud accounts, or showing ads and suggestions. This rule turns those features off or down so government information stays inside the government's systems, like not letting a delivery driver wander through the office and take notes.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers | DisableWebPnPDownload | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Internet Communication Management >> Internet Communication settings | Turn off downloading of print drivers over HTTP | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Users lose consumer conveniences such as Store apps, Microsoft-account sign-in and web results in search. Enterprise management may need a minimum telemetry level (e.g. for Windows Update for Business reports), so align the value with the STIG's allowed options.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\

Value Name: DisableWebPnPDownload

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Internet Communication Management >> Internet Communication settings >> "Turn off downloading of print drivers over HTTP" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Some features may communicate with the vendor, sending system information or downloading data or components for the feature. Turning off this capability will prevent potentially sensitive information from being sent outside the enterprise and uncontrolled updates to the system. This setting prevents the computer from downloading print driver packages over HTTP.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Some features may communicate with the vendor, sending system information or downloading data or components for the feature. Turning off this capability will prevent potentially sensitive information from being sent outside the enterprise and uncontrolled updates to the system. This setting prevents the client computer from printing over HTTP, which allows the computer to print to printers on the intranet as well as the internet.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253377 · WN11-CC-000115 · CAT II: Systems must at least attempt device authentication using certificates.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253377r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Systems must at least attempt device authentication using certificates.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kerberos*: The ticket-based sign-in system used by Windows domains and some Linux systems.
- *PKI / certificates*: Public Key Infrastructure: the system of digital ID certificates and trusted issuers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Kerberos\Parameters | DevicePKInitEnabled | REG_DWORD = 1 (or if the Value Name does not exist) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Kerberos | Support device authentication using certificate | "Not Configured or "Enabled" with either option selected in "Device authentication behavior using certificate:" |

**How it works:** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This requirement is applicable to domain-joined systems, for standalone systems this is NA.

The default behavior for "Support device authentication using certificate" is "Automatic".

If it exists and is configured with a value of "0", this is a finding.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Kerberos\Parameters\

Value Name: DevicePKInitEnabled
Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1 (or if the Value Name does not exist)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
This requirement is applicable to domain-joined systems, for standalone systems this is NA.

The default behavior for "Support device authentication using certificate" is "Automatic".

To correct this, configured the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Kerberos >> "Support device authentication using certificate" to "Not Configured or "Enabled" with either option selected in "Device authentication behavior using certificate:".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Using certificates to authenticate devices to the domain provides increased security over passwords. By default systems will attempt to authenticate using certificates and fall back to passwords if the domain controller does not support certificates for devices. This may also be configured to always use certificates for device authentication.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253378 · WN11-CC-000120 · CAT II: The network selection user interface (UI) must not be displayed on the logon screen.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253378r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The network selection user interface (UI) must not be displayed on the logon screen.

**Why it matters:** This decides what the sign-in screen shows and which shortcuts are allowed. For example, it hides the list of usernames, doesn't show who signed in last, and turns off "sign in automatically". It's like a hotel front desk that won't tell a stranger which room a guest is in.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System | DontDisplayNetworkSelectionUI | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon | Do not display network selection UI | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Security Options such as 'Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in' and 'Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL' (Disabled). Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon covers enumerating local users, convenience PIN and picture password. Credential User Interface >> 'Do not display the password reveal button' handles the reveal button.

**Operational impact:** Users will need to type their username in full and can't use convenience sign-in methods. Hiding restart buttons on the logon screen means console users need credentials to reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System\

Value Name: DontDisplayNetworkSelectionUI

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon >> "Do not display network selection UI" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enabling interaction with the network selection UI allows users to change connections to available networks without signing into Windows.

**Threat & control context:** The logon surface can leak information (usernames, the last logged-on user, local administrator lists) that cuts an attacker's effort in half, and convenience features (automatic logon, picture passwords, convenience PINs, password reveal buttons) weaken authentication assurance. These settings reduce information disclosure (AC-14, IA-6 authenticator feedback) and keep interactive logon on approved authenticators.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253380 · WN11-CC-000145 · CAT II: Users must be prompted for a password on resume from sleep (on battery).

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253380r1051049_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000373-GPOS-00156 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-002038 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-11 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-11 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Users must be prompted for a password on resume from sleep (on battery).

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Power\PowerSettings\0e796bdb-100d-47d6-a2d5-f7d2daa51f51 | DCSettingIndex | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Power Management >> Sleep Settings | Require a password when a computer wakes (on battery) | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set 'Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit' (InactivityTimeoutSecs <= 900) and 'Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior' (Lock Workstation). Personalization policies prevent the lock screen from showing slide shows or camera access.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Power\PowerSettings\0e796bdb-100d-47d6-a2d5-f7d2daa51f51\

Value Name: DCSettingIndex

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Power Management >> Sleep Settings >> "Require a password when a computer wakes (on battery)" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Authentication must always be required when accessing a system. This setting ensures the user is prompted for a password on resume from sleep (on battery).

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002038**: The organization requires users to reauthenticate upon organization-defined circumstances or situations requiring reauthentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-11 · Rev 4: IA-11 · Rev 3: n/a

---

### V-253382 · WN11-CC-000155 · CAT I: Solicited Remote Assistance must not be allowed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253382r1268233_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000138-GPOS-00069 |
| Topic | Remote Desktop & Remote Management |
| CCI | CCI-001090 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-4 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Solicited Remote Assistance must not be allowed.

**Why it matters:** Administrators can control computers from far away, as if they were sitting at the keyboard. This rule makes sure those remote connections are encrypted, require a proper sign-in every time, and can't be used to copy files around carelessly. It's like requiring a video-verified, recorded call before anyone can give orders over the phone.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services | fAllowToGetHelp | REG_DWORD = 0 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Remote Assistance | Configure Solicited Remote Assistance | "Disabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, RDP settings are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Remote Desktop Services >> Remote Desktop Session Host (Security / Device and Resource Redirection / Session Time Limits), and WinRM settings under Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM Client / WinRM Service). Verify WinRM with 'winrm get winrm/config'.

**Operational impact:** Disabling drive and clipboard redirection affects admin convenience. WinRM restrictions can break management tools that use Basic auth over HTTP (some older configuration-management and monitoring products), so move those to Kerberos or HTTPS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services\

Value Name: fAllowToGetHelp

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Remote Assistance >> "Configure Solicited Remote Assistance" to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Remote assistance allows another user to view or take control of the local session of a user. Solicited assistance is help that is specifically requested by the local user. This may allow unauthorized parties access to the resources on the computer.

**Threat & control context:** Remote-management protocols give interactive or programmatic control of a host and are a favored vector for both ransomware operators and insiders. Requirements include encrypted transport, no Basic/Digest authentication or unencrypted WinRM traffic, always prompting for credentials, no saved RDP passwords, no drive redirection, and session time limits. These implement AC-17 (remote access), AC-17(2) (confidentiality and integrity via encryption), SC-8 and AC-12 (session termination).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001090**: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.  
  Rev 5: SC-4 · Rev 4: SC-4 · Rev 3: SC-4

### V-253383 · WN11-CC-000165 · CAT II: Unauthenticated RPC clients must be restricted from connecting to the RPC server.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253383r971545_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000379-GPOS-00164 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-001967 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-3 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-3 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Unauthenticated RPC clients must be restricted from connecting to the RPC server.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Rpc | RestrictRemoteClients | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Remote Procedure Call | Restrict Unauthenticated RPC clients | "Enabled" and "Authenticated" |

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Rpc\

Value Name: RestrictRemoteClients

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Remote Procedure Call >> "Restrict Unauthenticated RPC clients" to "Enabled" and "Authenticated".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Configuring RPC to restrict unauthenticated RPC clients from connecting to the RPC server will prevent anonymous connections.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001967**: Authenticate organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection using bidirectional authentication that is cryptographically based.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 (1) · Rev 4: IA-3 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253384 · WN11-CC-000170 · CAT III: The setting to allow Microsoft accounts to be optional for modern style apps must be enabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253384r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The setting to allow Microsoft accounts to be optional for modern style apps must be enabled.

**Why it matters:** Modern computers like to "phone home", sending usage data to the manufacturer, syncing to personal cloud accounts, or showing ads and suggestions. This rule turns those features off or down so government information stays inside the government's systems, like not letting a delivery driver wander through the office and take notes.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System | MSAOptional | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> App Runtime | Allow Microsoft accounts | be optional" to "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Users lose consumer conveniences such as Store apps, Microsoft-account sign-in and web results in search. Enterprise management may need a minimum telemetry level (e.g. for Windows Update for Business reports), so align the value with the STIG's allowed options.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\

Value Name: MSAOptional

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000001 (1)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> App Runtime >> "Allow Microsoft accounts to be optional" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Control of credentials and the system must be maintained within the enterprise. Enabling this setting allows enterprise credentials to be used with modern style apps that support this, instead of Microsoft accounts.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253386 · WN11-CC-000180 · CAT I: Autoplay must be turned off for non-volume devices.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253386r958804_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000368-GPOS-00154 |
| Topic | Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless |
| CCI | CCI-001764 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Autoplay must be turned off for non-volume devices.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer | NoAutoplayfornonVolume | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies | Disallow Autoplay for non-volume devices | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer\

Value Name: NoAutoplayfornonVolume

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies >> "Disallow Autoplay for non-volume devices" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Allowing autoplay to execute may introduce malicious code to a system. Autoplay begins reading from a drive as soon as media is inserted in the drive. As a result, the setup file of programs or music on audio media may start. This setting will disable autoplay for non-volume devices (such as Media Transfer Protocol (MTP) devices).

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253389 · WN11-CC-000195 · CAT II: Enhanced anti-spoofing for facial recognition must be enabled on Windows 11.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253389r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Logon Screen & Desktop Settings, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Enhanced anti-spoofing for facial recognition must be enabled on this computer.

**Why it matters:** This decides what the sign-in screen shows and which shortcuts are allowed. For example, it hides the list of usernames, doesn't show who signed in last, and turns off "sign in automatically". It's like a hotel front desk that won't tell a stranger which room a guest is in.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Group Policy*: The central way Windows administrators push settings to many computers at once.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Policies\PassportForWork\Biometrics\   (For Intune-managed systems) | FacialFeaturesUseEnhancedAntiSpoofing  (For Intune-managed systems) | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Biometrics >> Facial Features | Configure enhanced anti-spoofing | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Security Options such as 'Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in' and 'Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL' (Disabled). Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon covers enumerating local users, convenience PIN and picture password. Credential User Interface >> 'Do not display the password reveal button' handles the reveal button.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Users will need to type their username in full and can't use convenience sign-in methods. Hiding restart buttons on the logon screen means console users need credentials to reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Biometrics\FacialFeatures\   (For GPO-managed systems)
Or
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Policies\PassportForWork\Biometrics\   (For Intune-managed systems)

Value Name: EnhancedAntiSpoofing
Or
Value Name: FacialFeaturesUseEnhancedAntiSpoofing  (For Intune-managed systems)

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000001 (1)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
For GPO-managed systems:

Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Biometrics >> Facial Features >> "Configure enhanced anti-spoofing" to "Enabled".

For Intune-managed systems:

Revise the Intune policy to enable enhanced anti-spoofing for Facial Features.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enhanced anti-spoofing provides additional protections when using facial recognition with devices that support it.

Note: A different registry location is needed when systems are managed by Intune versus GPO.

**Threat & control context:** The logon surface can leak information (usernames, the last logged-on user, local administrator lists) that cuts an attacker's effort in half, and convenience features (automatic logon, picture passwords, convenience PINs, password reveal buttons) weaken authentication assurance. These settings reduce information disclosure (AC-14, IA-6 authenticator feedback) and keep interactive logon on approved authenticators.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b
