### V-253420 · WN11-CC-000355 · CAT II: The Windows Remote Management (WinRM) service must not store RunAs credentials.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253420r1051055_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000373-GPOS-00156 |
| Topic | Credential Storage & Password Hashing, Remote Desktop & Remote Management |
| CCI | CCI-002038 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-11 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-11 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Windows Remote Management (WinRM) service must not store RunAs credentials.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *WinRM*: A Windows service that lets administrators run commands on a computer over the network.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WinRM\Service | DisableRunAs | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM) >> WinRM Service | Disallow WinRM from storing RunAs credentials | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** Relevant Windows settings include 'Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' (NoLMHash), 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' (Disabled), and 'Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache' (CachedLogonsCount).

**Also related (Remote Desktop & Remote Management):** On Windows, RDP settings are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Remote Desktop Services >> Remote Desktop Session Host (Security / Device and Resource Redirection / Session Time Limits), and WinRM settings under Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM Client / WinRM Service). Verify WinRM with 'winrm get winrm/config'.

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WinRM\Service\

Value Name: DisableRunAs

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM) >> WinRM Service >> "Disallow WinRM from storing RunAs credentials" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Storage of administrative credentials could allow unauthorized access. Disallowing the storage of RunAs credentials for Windows Remote Management will prevent them from being used with plug-ins.

**Threat & control context:** When a host is compromised, stored credential material is the attacker's path to lateral movement. Weak or reversible storage (LM hashes, reversible encryption, low-iteration hashes, excessive cached domain logons) turns a single compromise into credential recovery for many accounts. IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials; T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002038**: The organization requires users to reauthenticate upon organization-defined circumstances or situations requiring reauthentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-11 · Rev 4: IA-11 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253421 · WN11-CC-000360 · CAT II: The Windows Remote Management (WinRM) client must not use Digest authentication.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253421r958510_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000125-GPOS-00065 |
| Topic | Remote Desktop & Remote Management |
| CCI | CCI-000877 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | MA-4 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | MA-4 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | MA-4 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Windows Remote Management (WinRM) client must not use Digest authentication.

**Why it matters:** Administrators can control computers from far away, as if they were sitting at the keyboard. This rule makes sure those remote connections are encrypted, require a proper sign-in every time, and can't be used to copy files around carelessly. It's like requiring a video-verified, recorded call before anyone can give orders over the phone.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *WinRM*: A Windows service that lets administrators run commands on a computer over the network.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WinRM\Client | AllowDigest | REG_DWORD = 0 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM) >> WinRM Client | Disallow Digest authentication | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, RDP settings are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Remote Desktop Services >> Remote Desktop Session Host (Security / Device and Resource Redirection / Session Time Limits), and WinRM settings under Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM Client / WinRM Service). Verify WinRM with 'winrm get winrm/config'.

**Operational impact:** Disabling drive and clipboard redirection affects admin convenience. WinRM restrictions can break management tools that use Basic auth over HTTP (some older configuration-management and monitoring products), so move those to Kerberos or HTTPS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WinRM\Client\

Value Name: AllowDigest

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM) >> WinRM Client >> "Disallow Digest authentication" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Digest authentication is not as strong as other options and may be subject to man-in-the-middle attacks.

**Threat & control context:** Remote-management protocols give interactive or programmatic control of a host and are a favored vector for both ransomware operators and insiders. Requirements include encrypted transport, no Basic/Digest authentication or unencrypted WinRM traffic, always prompting for credentials, no saved RDP passwords, no drive redirection, and session time limits. These implement AC-17 (remote access), AC-17(2) (confidentiality and integrity via encryption), SC-8 and AC-12 (session termination).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000877**: Employ strong authentication in the establishment of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 c · Rev 4: MA-4 c · Rev 3: MA-4 c

### V-253422 · WN11-CC-000365 · CAT II: Windows 11 must be configured to prevent Windows apps from being activated by voice while the system is locked.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253422r1270952_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000028-GPOS-00009 |
| Topic | Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-000056 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-11 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-11 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-11 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to prevent Windows apps from being activated by voice while the system is locked.

**Why it matters:** Modern computers like to "phone home", sending usage data to the manufacturer, syncing to personal cloud accounts, or showing ads and suggestions. This rule turns those features off or down so government information stays inside the government's systems, like not letting a delivery driver wander through the office and take notes.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppPrivacy | LetAppsActivateWithVoiceAboveLock | REG_DWORD = 0x00000002 (2) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> App Privacy | Let Windows apps activate with voice while the system is locked | "Enabled" with Default for all Apps: set to "Force Deny" |

**How it works:** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Users lose consumer conveniences such as Store apps, Microsoft-account sign-in and web results in search. Enterprise management may need a minimum telemetry level (e.g. for Windows Update for Business reports), so align the value with the STIG's allowed options.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppPrivacy\
Value Name: LetAppsActivateWithVoiceAboveLock

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000002 (2)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> App Privacy >> "Let Windows apps activate with voice while the system is locked" to "Enabled" with Default for all Apps: set to "Force Deny".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Allowing Windows apps to be activated by voice from the lock screen could allow for unauthorized use. Requiring logon will ensure the apps are used only by authorized personnel.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000056**: Retain the device lock until the user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 b · Rev 4: AC-11 b · Rev 3: AC-11 b

### V-253423 · WN11-CC-000370 · CAT II: The convenience PIN for Windows 11 must be disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253423r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The convenience PIN for this computer must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** This decides what the sign-in screen shows and which shortcuts are allowed. For example, it hides the list of usernames, doesn't show who signed in last, and turns off "sign in automatically". It's like a hotel front desk that won't tell a stranger which room a guest is in.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon | Set "Turn on convenience PIN sign-in | "Disabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Security Options such as 'Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in' and 'Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL' (Disabled). Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon covers enumerating local users, convenience PIN and picture password. Credential User Interface >> 'Do not display the password reveal button' handles the reveal button.

**Operational impact:** Users will need to type their username in full and can't use convenience sign-in methods. Hiding restart buttons on the logon screen means console users need credentials to reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System

Value Name: AllowDomainPINLogon
Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value data: 0
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Disable the convenience PIN sign-in.

To correct this, configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon >> Set "Turn on convenience PIN sign-in" to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** This policy controls whether a domain user can sign in using a convenience PIN to prevent enabling (Password Stuffer).

**Threat & control context:** The logon surface can leak information (usernames, the last logged-on user, local administrator lists) that cuts an attacker's effort in half, and convenience features (automatic logon, picture passwords, convenience PINs, password reveal buttons) weaken authentication assurance. These settings reduce information disclosure (AC-14, IA-6 authenticator feedback) and keep interactive logon on approved authenticators.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253425 · WN11-CC-000390 · CAT III: Windows 11 must be configured to prevent users from receiving suggestions for third-party or additional applications.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253425r1259997_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | PowerShell & Scripting Security |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to prevent users from receiving suggestions for third-party or additional applications.

**Why it matters:** PowerShell is a powerful tool for automating tasks on Windows, which also makes it a favorite of hackers. This rule makes the computer keep a detailed record of every PowerShell command that runs, like a CCTV camera pointed at the most powerful tool in the workshop.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CloudContent | DisableThirdPartySuggestions | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) |
| Group Policy | User Configuration >> Administrative Templates. >> Windows Components >> Cloud Content | Do not suggest third-party content in Windows spotlight | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, configure these under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Windows PowerShell: 'Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging' (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging EnableScriptBlockLogging = 1) and 'Turn on PowerShell Transcription'. Logs go to Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational. Write transcripts to a protected, centrally collected location.

**Operational impact:** Script-block logs can be large and may capture secrets embedded in scripts. Size the PowerShell Operational log appropriately and restrict who can read it.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This Check must be performed for each interactive user profile on the system.
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_CURRENT_USER
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CloudContent\

Value Name: DisableThirdPartySuggestions

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000001 (1)

Note: This requirement is applicable to profiles for interactive logins. It is not applicable for Service accounts.

To determine the system's enabled user profiles:
Run "PowerShell" as an administrator.

Execute the following command:
Get-LocalUser | Where-Object {$_.Enabled -eq $true}
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
For each user profile on the system, configure the policy value for User Configuration >> Administrative Templates. >> Windows Components >> Cloud Content >> "Do not suggest third-party content in Windows spotlight" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Windows spotlight features may suggest apps and content from third-party software publishers in addition to Microsoft apps and content.

**Threat & control context:** PowerShell is the dominant 'living off the land' tool in Windows intrusions. Script Block Logging (event 4104) records de-obfuscated code as it executes, and Transcription records full session input and output. Together they provide high-fidelity detection content for AU-2/AU-12 and SI-4. Removing PowerShell 2.0 prevents downgrade attacks that bypass these logs and AMSI.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell; T1059.005 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic; T1562.003 Impair Defenses: Impair Command History Logging

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.

```text
Determine if IE11 is installed or enabled on Windows 11 semi-annual channel.

If IE11 is installed or not disabled on Windows 11 semi-annual channel, this is a finding.

If IE11 is installed on an unsupported operating system and is enabled or installed, this is a finding.

For more information, visit: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/lifecycle/faq/internet-explorer-microsoft-edge#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-internet-explorer-
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
For Windows 11 semi-annual channel, remove or disable the IE11 application.

To disable IE11 as a standalone browser:

Set the policy value for "Computer Configuration/Administrative Templates/Windows Components/Internet Explorer/Disable Internet Explorer 11 as a standalone browser" to "Enabled" with the option value set to "Never".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Internet Explorer 11 (IE11) is not supported on Windows 11 semi-annual channel.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253426 · WN11-EP-000310 · CAT II: Windows 11 Kernel (Direct Memory Access) DMA Protection must be enabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253426r991580_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00216 |
| Topic | Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's Kernel (Direct Memory Access) DMA Protection must be enabled.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Kernel DMA Protection | DeviceEnumerationPolicy | REG_DWORD = 0 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Kernel DMA Protection | Enumeration policy for external devices incompatible with Kernel DMA Protection | "Enabled" with "Enumeration Policy" set to "Block All" |

**How it works:** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Kernel DMA Protection

Value Name: DeviceEnumerationPolicy
Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Kernel DMA Protection >> "Enumeration policy for external devices incompatible with Kernel DMA Protection" to "Enabled" with "Enumeration Policy" set to "Block All".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Kernel DMA Protection to protect PCs against drive-by Direct Memory Access (DMA) attacks using PCI hot plug devices connected to Thunderbolt 3 ports. Drive-by DMA attacks can lead to disclosure of sensitive information residing on a PC, or even injection of malware that allows attackers to bypass the lock screen or control PCs remotely.

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-253427 · WN11-PK-000005 · CAT II: The DoW Root CA certificates must be installed in the Trusted Root Store.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253427r1256656_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000066-GPOS-00034 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000185 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (2) (b) (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (2) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (2) |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The DoW Root CA certificates must be installed in the Trusted Root Store.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).
- *PKI / certificates*: Public Key Infrastructure: the system of digital ID certificates and trusted issuers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the DoW Root CA certificates are installed as Trusted Root Certification Authorities.

The certificates referenced below apply to unclassified systems; refer to PKE documentation for other networks.

Run "PowerShell" as an administrator.

Execute the following command:

Get-ChildItem -Path Cert:Localmachine\root | Where Subject -Like "*DoD*" | FL Subject, NotAfter

If valid DoW Root CA certificates (such as those below) are not displayed, this is a finding.

Note: The Common Names (CN) below are examples. Verify the "CN" displayed is a DoW Root CA and is not expired.

Subject: CN=DoD Root CA 3, OU=PKI, OU=DoD, O=U.S. Government, C=US
NotAfter: 12/30/2029

Subject: CN=DoD Root CA 5, OU=PKI, OU=DoD, O=U.S. Government, C=US
NotAfter: 6/14/2041

Subject: CN=DoD Root CA 6 OU=PKI, OU=DoD, O=U.S. Government, C=US
NotAfter: 1/24/2053

Alternately, use the Certificates MMC snap-in:

Run "MMC".

Select "File" and "Add/Remove Snap-in".

Select "Certificates" and click "Add".

Select "Computer account" and click "Next".

Select "Local computer: (the computer this console is running on)" and click "Finish".

Click "OK".

Expand "Certificates" and navigate to Trusted Root Certification Authorities >> Certificates.

For each of the DoW Root CA certificates listed:

Right-click on the certificate and select "Open".

Select the "Details" tab.

Verify the Expiration Date is a future date.

Scroll to the bottom and select "Subject".

If valid (unexpired) DoW Root CA certificates (such as those below) are not listed, this is a finding.

DoD Root CA 3
DoD Root CA 5
DoD Root CA 6
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install valid (unexpired) DoW Root CA certificates.

The list below is not to be treated as exhaustive. The STIG should not be used as a definitive resource for the organizationally approved certificates for the systems.

DoD Root CA 3
DoD Root CA 5
DoD Root CA 6

The InstallRoot tool is available on Cyber Exchange at https://cyber.mil/pki-pke/tools-configuration-files. Certificate bundles published by the PKI can be found at https://crl.gds.disa.mil/.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To ensure secure DoW websites and DoW-signed code are properly validated, the system must trust the DoW Root Certificate Authorities (CAs). The DoW root certificates will ensure that the trust chain is established for server certificates issued from the DoW CAs.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000185**: For public key-based authentication, validate certificates by constructing and verifying a certification path to an accepted trust anchor including checking certificate status information.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (2) (b) (1) · Rev 4: IA-5 (2) (a) · Rev 3: IA-5 (2)

| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Default permissions for the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE registry hive must be maintained.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Registry*: Windows' internal database of settings.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the default registry permissions for the keys note below of the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE hive.

If any non-privileged groups such as Everyone, Users or Authenticated Users have greater than Read permission, this is a finding.

Run "Regedit".
Right click on the registry areas noted below.
Select "Permissions..." and the "Advanced" button.

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SECURITY
Type - "Allow" for all
Inherited from - "None" for all
Principal - Access - Applies to
SYSTEM - Full Control - This key and subkeys
Administrators - Special - This key and subkeys

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE
Type - "Allow" for all
Inherited from - "None" for all
Principal - Access - Applies to
Users - Read - This key and subkeys
Administrators - Full Control - This key and subkeys
SYSTEM - Full Control - This key and subkeys
CREATOR OWNER - Full Control - This key and subkeys
ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES - Read - This key and subkeys

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM
Type - "Allow" for all
Inherited from - "None" for all
Principal - Access - Applies to
Users - Read - This key and subkeys
Administrators - Full Control - This key and subkeys
SYSTEM - Full Control - This key and subkeys
CREATOR OWNER - Full Control - This key and subkeys
ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES - Read - This key and subkeys

Other subkeys under the noted keys may also be sampled. There may be some instances where non-privileged groups have greater than read permission.

Microsoft has given Read permission to the SOFTWARE and SYSTEM registry keys in later versions of Windows 11 to the following SID, this is currently not a finding.

S-1-15-3-1024-1065365936-1281604716-3511738428-1654721687-432734479-3232135806-4053264122-3456934681

If the defaults have not been changed, these are not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Maintain the default permissions for the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE registry hive.

The default permissions of the higher level keys are noted below.

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SECURITY
Type - "Allow" for all
Inherited from - "None" for all
Principal - Access - Applies to
SYSTEM - Full Control - This key and subkeys
Administrators - Special - This key and subkeys

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE
Type - "Allow" for all
Inherited from - "None" for all
Principal - Access - Applies to
Users - Read - This key and subkeys
Administrators - Full Control - This key and subkeys
SYSTEM - Full Control - This key and subkeys
CREATOR OWNER - Full Control - This key and subkeys
ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES - Read - This key and subkeys

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM
Type - "Allow" for all
Inherited from - "None" for all
Principal - Access - Applies to
Users - Read - This key and subkeys
Administrators - Full Control - This key and subkeys
SYSTEM - Full Control - This key and subkeys
CREATOR OWNER - Full Control - This key and subkeys
ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES - Read - This key and subkeys

Microsoft has also given read permission to the SOFTWARE and SYSTEM registry keys in later versions of Windows 11 to the following SID.

S-1-15-3-1024-1065365936-1281604716-3511738428-1654721687-432734479-3232135806-4053264122-3456934681
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The registry is integral to the function, security, and stability of the Windows system. Changing the system's registry permissions allows the possibility of unauthorized and anonymous modification to the operating system.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253433 · WN11-SO-000010 · CAT II: The built-in guest account must be disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253433r958504_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000121-GPOS-00062 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening, Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-000804 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-8 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The built-in guest account must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Accounts: Guest account status | "Disabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows these are Security Options ('Accounts: Rename administrator account', 'Accounts: Guest account status', 'Accounts: Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only') plus LAPS for unique, rotated local administrator passwords.

**Also related (Account Lifecycle Management):** On Windows, use 'Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 35' for domain accounts. For local accounts, review 'Get-LocalUser' (LastLogon, PasswordExpires) and disable or delete accounts that aren't needed. Shared accounts require ISSO-documented justification.

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options.

If the value for "Accounts: Guest account status" is not set to "Disabled", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Accounts: Guest account status" to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A system faces an increased vulnerability threat if the built-in guest account is not disabled. This account is a known account that exists on all Windows systems and cannot be deleted. This account is initialized during the installation of the operating system with no password assigned.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000804**: Uniquely identify and authenticate non-organizational users or processes acting on behalf of non-organizational users.  
  Rev 5: IA-8 · Rev 4: IA-8 · Rev 3: IA-8

### V-253437 · WN11-SO-000030 · CAT II: Audit policy using subcategories must be enabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253437r1268225_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000169 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Audit policy using subcategories must be enabled.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa | SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\

Value Name: SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior. This setting allows administrators to enable more precise auditing capabilities.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000169**: Provide audit record generation capability for the event types the system is capable of auditing as defined in AU-2 a on organization-defined information system components.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 a · Rev 4: AU-12 a · Rev 3: AU-12 a

### V-253438 · WN11-SO-000035 · CAT II: Outgoing secure channel traffic must be encrypted or signed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253438r958908_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000423-GPOS-00187 |
| Topic | Active Directory & Domain Controller Security |
| CCI | CCI-002418, CCI-002421 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-8, SC-8 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-8, SC-8 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Outgoing secure channel traffic must be encrypted or signed.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters | RequireSignOrSeal | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always) | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters\

Value Name: RequireSignOrSeal

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Requests sent on the secure channel are authenticated, and sensitive information (such as passwords) is encrypted, but not all information is encrypted. If this policy is enabled, outgoing secure channel traffic will be encrypted and signed.

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

### V-253439 · WN11-SO-000040 · CAT II: Outgoing secure channel traffic must be encrypted.

| Field | Value |

| Rule ID | `SV-253439r958908_rule` |

| SRG | SRG-OS-000423-GPOS-00187 |

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-8, SC-8 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-8, SC-8 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Outgoing secure channel traffic must be encrypted.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters | SealSecureChannel | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Domain member: Digitally encrypt secure channel data (when possible) | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters\

Value Name: SealSecureChannel

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Domain member: Digitally encrypt secure channel data (when possible)" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Requests sent on the secure channel are authenticated, and sensitive information (such as passwords) is encrypted, but not all information is encrypted. If this policy is enabled, outgoing secure channel traffic will be encrypted.

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002418**: Protect the confidentiality and/or integrity of transmitted information.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 · Rev 4: SC-8 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002421**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of information and/or detect changes to information during transmission.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 (1) · Rev 4: SC-8 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253442 · WN11-SO-000055 · CAT III: The maximum age for machine account passwords must be configured to 30 days or less.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253442r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse, Active Directory & Domain Controller Security |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The maximum age for machine account passwords must be configured to 30 days or less.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters | MaximumPasswordAge | REG_DWORD = 0x0000001e (30) (or less, excluding 0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Domain member: Maximum machine account password age | "30" or less (excluding 0 which is unacceptable) |

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy: 'Maximum password age', 'Minimum password age', 'Enforce password history'. Domain values come from the Default Domain Policy or PSOs.

**Also related (Active Directory & Domain Controller Security):** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
(remove)This is the default configuration for this setting (30 days).

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters\

Value Name: MaximumPasswordAge

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x0000001e (30) (or less, excluding 0)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
This is the default configuration for this setting (30 days).

Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Domain member: Maximum machine account password age" to "30" or less (excluding 0 which is unacceptable).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Computer account passwords are changed automatically on a regular basis. This setting controls the maximum password age that a machine account may have. This setting must be set to no more than 30 days, ensuring the machine changes its password monthly.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing; T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253444 · WN11-SO-000070 · CAT II: The machine inactivity limit must be set to 15 minutes, locking the system with the screensaver.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253444r958636_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000279-GPOS-00109 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-001133, CCI-002361 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-10, AC-12 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-10, AC-12 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-10 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The machine inactivity limit must be set to 15 minutes, locking the system with the screensaver.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System | InactivityTimeoutSecs | REG_DWORD = 0x00000384 (900) (or less, excluding "0" which is effectively disabled) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit | "900" seconds" or less, excluding "0" which is effectively disabled |

**How it works:** On Windows, set 'Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit' (InactivityTimeoutSecs <= 900) and 'Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior' (Lock Workstation). Personalization policies prevent the lock screen from showing slide shows or camera access.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\

Value Name: InactivityTimeoutSecs

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000384 (900) (or less, excluding "0" which is effectively disabled)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit" to "900" seconds" or less, excluding "0" which is effectively disabled.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unattended systems are susceptible to unauthorized use and must be locked when unattended. The screen saver must be set at a maximum of 15 minutes and be password protected. This protects critical and sensitive data from exposure to unauthorized personnel with physical access to the computer.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000279-GPOS-00109, SRG-OS-000163-GPOS-00072

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001133**: Terminate the network connection associated with a communications session at the end of the session or after an organization-defined time period of inactivity.  
  Rev 5: SC-10 · Rev 4: SC-10 · Rev 3: SC-10
- **CCI-002361**: Automatically terminate a user session after organization-defined conditions or trigger events requiring session disconnect.  
  Rev 5: AC-12 · Rev 4: AC-12 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253445 · WN11-SO-000075 · CAT II: The required legal notice must be configured to display before console logon.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253445r1268218_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000024-GPOS-00007 |
| Topic | Logon Banner & Consent Notice |
| CCI | CCI-000044, CCI-000048, CCI-000050 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 a, AC-8 a, AC-8 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 a, AC-8 a, AC-8 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-7 a, AC-8 a, AC-8 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The required legal notice must be configured to display before console logon.

**Why it matters:** Before anyone can sign in, the computer shows a warning message saying the system belongs to the government, that activity is monitored, and that using it means you agree to that. Think of it like the "this area is under video surveillance" sign at the entrance to a building: it doesn't lock the door, but it makes the rules clear and discourages misuse.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Interactive logon: Message text for users attempting to log on | the following |

**How it works:** On Windows the banner is configured through Security Options: 'Interactive logon: Message title for users attempting to log on' and 'Interactive logon: Message text for users attempting to log on' (registry LegalNoticeCaption / LegalNoticeText under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System).

**Operational impact:** No functional impact. Automated logons and kiosk workflows will need to acknowledge the banner, and some scanners compare the text byte-for-byte, so copy it from the STIG rather than retyping it.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:
Note: If configuring this policy via a Policy Configuration Service Provider (CSP), additional steps are needed (see Fix Text).

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\

Value Name: LegalNoticeText

Value Type: REG_SZ
Value:
You are accessing a U.S. Government (USG) Information System (IS) that is provided for USG-authorized use only.

By using this IS (which includes any device attached to this IS), you consent to the following conditions:

-The USG routinely intercepts and monitors communications on this IS for purposes including, but not limited to, penetration testing, COMSEC monitoring, network operations and defense, personnel misconduct (PM), law enforcement (LE), and counterintelligence (CI) investigations.

-At any time, the USG may inspect and seize data stored on this IS.

-Communications using, or data stored on, this IS are not private, are subject to routine monitoring, interception, and search, and may be disclosed or used for any USG-authorized purpose.

-This IS includes security measures (e.g., authentication and access controls) to protect USG interests--not for your personal benefit or privacy.

-Notwithstanding the above, using this IS does not constitute consent to PM, LE or CI investigative searching or monitoring of the content of privileged communications, or work product, related to personal representation or services by attorneys, psychotherapists, or clergy, and their assistants. Such communications and work product are private and confidential. See User Agreement for details.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Interactive logon: Message text for users attempting to log on" to the following.

You are accessing a U.S. Government (USG) Information System (IS) that is provided for USG-authorized use only.

By using this IS (which includes any device attached to this IS), you consent to the following conditions:

-The USG routinely intercepts and monitors communications on this IS for purposes including, but not limited to, penetration testing, COMSEC monitoring, network operations and defense, personnel misconduct (PM), law enforcement (LE), and counterintelligence (CI) investigations.

-At any time, the USG may inspect and seize data stored on this IS.

-Communications using, or data stored on, this IS are not private, are subject to routine monitoring, interception, and search, and may be disclosed or used for any USG-authorized purpose.

-This IS includes security measures (e.g., authentication and access controls) to protect USG interests--not for your personal benefit or privacy.

-Notwithstanding the above, using this IS does not constitute consent to PM, LE or CI investigative searching or monitoring of the content of privileged communications, or work product, related to personal representation or services by attorneys, psychotherapists, or clergy, and their assistants. Such communications and work product are private and confidential. See User Agreement for details.

Note: For MDM/Intune implementation, when configuring this policy via a Policy Configuration Service Provider (CSP), both the "Message text" and the "Interactive logon: Message title for users attempting to log on" must be configured to enable the legal notice to be displayed. It is recommended to set the "Message title" to a non-blank value, such as "U.S. Government Warning" or a period (".").
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Failure to display the logon banner prior to a logon attempt will negate legal proceedings resulting from unauthorized access to system resources.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000024-GPOS-00007, SRG-OS-000228-GPOS-00088, SRG-OS-000024-GPOS-00007

**Threat & control context:** A notice-and-consent banner is a legal and deterrence control rather than a technical barrier. It establishes that users have no expectation of privacy, which supports monitoring, incident response and prosecution, and it satisfies AC-8 (System Use Notification). Assessors verify the exact approved DoD text, that it appears for every access path (console, GUI, SSH and other remote sessions), and that the user must acknowledge it before the session continues.

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a
- **CCI-000048**: Display an organization-defined system use notification message or banner to users before granting access to the system that provides privacy and security notices consistent with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidelines.  
  Rev 5: AC-8 a · Rev 4: AC-8 a · Rev 3: AC-8 a
- **CCI-000050**: Retain the notification message or banner on the screen until users acknowledge the usage conditions and take explicit actions to log on to or further access the system.  
  Rev 5: AC-8 b · Rev 4: AC-8 b · Rev 3: AC-8 b
