### V-253447 · WN11-SO-000085 · CAT III: Caching of logon credentials must be limited.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253447r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Credential Storage & Password Hashing |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Caching of logon credentials must be limited.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon | CachedLogonsCount | REG_SZ = 10 (or less) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache (in case domain controller is not available) | "10" logons or less |

**How it works:** Relevant Windows settings include 'Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' (NoLMHash), 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' (Disabled), and 'Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache' (CachedLogonsCount).

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This is the default configuration for this setting (10 logons to cache).

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\

Value Name: CachedLogonsCount

Value Type: REG_SZ
Value: 10 (or less)

This setting only applies to domain-joined systems, however, it is configured by default on all systems.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
This is the default configuration for this setting (10 logons to cache).

Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache (in case domain controller is not available)" to "10" logons or less.

This setting only applies to domain-joined systems, however, it is configured by default on all systems.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The default Windows configuration caches the last logon credentials for users who log on interactively to a system. This feature is provided for system availability reasons, such as the user's machine being disconnected from the network or domain controllers being unavailable. Even though the credential cache is well-protected, if a system is attacked, an unauthorized individual may isolate the password to a domain user account using a password-cracking program and gain access to the domain.

**Threat & control context:** When a host is compromised, stored credential material is the attacker's path to lateral movement. Weak or reversible storage (LM hashes, reversible encryption, low-iteration hashes, excessive cached domain logons) turns a single compromise into credential recovery for many accounts. IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

---

### V-253448 · WN11-SO-000095 · CAT II: The Smart Card removal option must be configured to Force Logoff or Lock Workstation.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253448r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout, Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Smart Card removal option must be configured to Force Logoff or Lock Workstation.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon | SCRemoveOption | REG_SZ = 1 (Lock Workstation) or 2 (Force Logoff) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior | "Lock Workstation" or "Force Logoff" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set 'Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit' (InactivityTimeoutSecs <= 900) and 'Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior' (Lock Workstation). Personalization policies prevent the lock screen from showing slide shows or camera access.

**Also related (Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication):** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\

Value Name: SCRemoveOption

Value Type: REG_SZ
Value: 1 (Lock Workstation) or 2 (Force Logoff)

This can be left not configured or set to "No action" on workstations with the following conditions. This must be documented with the ISSO.
-The setting cannot be configured due to mission needs, or because it interferes with applications.
-Policy must be in place that users manually lock workstations when leaving them unattended.
-The screen saver is properly configured to lock as required.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior" to "Lock Workstation" or "Force Logoff".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unattended systems are susceptible to unauthorized use and must be locked. Configuring a system to lock when a smart card is removed will ensure the system is inaccessible when unattended.

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253449 · WN11-SO-000100 · CAT II: The Windows SMB client must be configured to always perform SMB packet signing.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253449r958908_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000423-GPOS-00187 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-002418 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The Windows SMB client must be configured to always perform SMB packet signing.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SMB*: Server Message Block: the protocol Windows uses for file and printer sharing.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanWorkstation\Parameters | RequireSecuritySignature | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always) | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanWorkstation\Parameters\

Value Name: RequireSecuritySignature

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The server message block (SMB) protocol provides the basis for many network operations. Digitally signed SMB packets aid in preventing man-in-the-middle attacks. If this policy is enabled, the SMB client will only communicate with an SMB server that performs SMB packet signing.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002418**: Protect the confidentiality and/or integrity of transmitted information.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 · Rev 4: SC-8 · Rev 3: n/a

| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts must not be allowed.

**Why it matters:** When you log into a Windows network, your computer and the server trade secret "handshakes" to prove who you are. Older handshakes are easy for attackers to fake or steal. This rule switches off the old, weak handshakes and protects the part of memory where Windows keeps your sign-in secrets, like retiring an old ID badge design that was easy to forge.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa | RestrictAnonymousSAM | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). Key settings include 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' (LmCompatibilityLevel = 5), 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos', 'Minimum session security for NTLM SSP', WDigest 'UseLogonCredential' = 0, and Credential Guard via Device Guard >> 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security'. Verify with 'gpresult /h' or the registry paths shown in the check.

**Also related (File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access):** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\

Value Name: RestrictAnonymousSAM

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts allows anonymous log on users (null session connections) to list all accounts names, thus providing a list of potential points to attack the system.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253454 · WN11-SO-000150 · CAT I: Anonymous enumeration of shares must be restricted.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253454r1268233_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000138-GPOS-00069 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-001090 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-4 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Anonymous enumeration of shares must be restricted.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa | RestrictAnonymous | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\

Value Name: RestrictAnonymous

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Allowing anonymous logon users (null session connections) to list all account names and enumerate all shared resources can provide a map of potential points to attack the system.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001090**: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.  
  Rev 5: SC-4 · Rev 4: SC-4 · Rev 3: SC-4

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

```text
Value Name: RestrictRemoteSAM

Value Type: REG_SZ
Value: O:BAG:BAD:(A;;RC;;;BA)

Vendor documentation must support the requirement for having the user right.
The requirement must be documented with the ISSO.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Navigate to the policy Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM".

Add "Administrators" in "Group or user names:" if it is not already listed (this is the default).

Select "Administrators" in "Group or user names:".

Select "Allow" for "Remote Access" in "Permissions for "Administrators".

Click "OK".

The "Security descriptor:" must be populated with "O:BAG:BAD:(A;;RC;;;BA) for the policy to be enforced.
```

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\LSA\pku2u\

Value Name: AllowOnlineID

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Network security: Allow PKU2U authentication requests to this computer to use online identities" to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** PKU2U is a peer-to-peer authentication protocol.  This setting prevents online identities from authenticating to domain-joined systems. Authentication will be centrally managed with Windows user accounts.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253460 · WN11-SO-000190 · CAT II: Kerberos encryption types must be configured to prevent the use of DES and RC4 encryption suites.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253460r1268232_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000120-GPOS-00061 |
| Topic | Windows Authentication Protocols (NTLM, Kerberos, LSA) |
| CCI | CCI-000803 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Kerberos encryption types must be configured to prevent the use of DES and RC4 encryption suites.

**Why it matters:** When you log into a Windows network, your computer and the server trade secret "handshakes" to prove who you are. Older handshakes are easy for attackers to fake or steal. This rule switches off the old, weak handshakes and protects the part of memory where Windows keeps your sign-in secrets, like retiring an old ID badge design that was easy to forge.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kerberos*: The ticket-based sign-in system used by Windows domains and some Linux systems.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Kerberos\Parameters | SupportedEncryptionTypes | REG_DWORD = 0x7ffffff8 (2147483640) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos | Only: AES128_HMAC_SHA1, AES256_HMAC_SHA1, Future encryption types |

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). Key settings include 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' (LmCompatibilityLevel = 5), 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos', 'Minimum session security for NTLM SSP', WDigest 'UseLogonCredential' = 0, and Credential Guard via Device Guard >> 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security'. Verify with 'gpresult /h' or the registry paths shown in the check.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Kerberos\Parameters\

Value Name: SupportedEncryptionTypes

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x7ffffff8 (2147483640)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos" to "Enabled" with only the following selected:

AES128_HMAC_SHA1
AES256_HMAC_SHA1
Future encryption types
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Certain encryption types are no longer considered secure. This setting configures a minimum encryption type for Kerberos, preventing the use of the DES and RC4 encryption suites.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000803**: Implement mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module that meet the requirements of applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance for such authentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-7 · Rev 4: IA-7 · Rev 3: IA-7

### V-253461 · WN11-SO-000195 · CAT I: The system must be configured to prevent the storage of the LAN Manager hash of passwords.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253461r1051056_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041 |
| Topic | Credential Storage & Password Hashing |
| CCI | CCI-004062, CCI-000196 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The system must be configured to prevent the storage of the LAN Manager hash of passwords.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *NTLM / LAN Manager*: Older Windows sign-in methods that are weaker than modern Kerberos.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa | NoLMHash | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** Relevant Windows settings include 'Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' (NoLMHash), 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' (Disabled), and 'Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache' (CachedLogonsCount).

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\

Value Name: NoLMHash

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The LAN Manager hash uses a weak encryption algorithm and there are several tools available that use this hash to retrieve account passwords. This setting controls whether or not a LAN Manager hash of the password is stored in the SAM the next time the password is changed.

**Threat & control context:** When a host is compromised, stored credential material is the attacker's path to lateral movement. Weak or reversible storage (LM hashes, reversible encryption, low-iteration hashes, excessive cached domain logons) turns a single compromise into credential recovery for many accounts. IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004062**: For password-based authentication, store passwords using an approved salted key derivation function, preferably using a keyed hash.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000196**: The information system, for password-based authentication, stores only cryptographically-protected passwords.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (c) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (c)

### V-253463 · WN11-SO-000210 · CAT II: The system must be configured to the required LDAP client signing level.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253463r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Active Directory & Domain Controller Security, File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The system must be configured to the required LDAP client signing level.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *LDAP*: A protocol for looking up users and groups in a central directory.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LDAP | LDAPClientIntegrity | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Network security: LDAP client signing requirements | "Negotiate signing" at a minimum |

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Also related (File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access):** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LDAP\

Value Name: LDAPClientIntegrity

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Network security: LDAP client signing requirements" to "Negotiate signing" at a minimum.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** This setting controls the signing requirements for LDAP clients. This setting must be set to Negotiate signing or Require signing, depending on the environment and type of LDAP server in use.

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "Network security: Minimum session security for NTLM SSP based (including secure RPC) servers" to "Require NTLMv2 session security" and "Require 128-bit encryption" (all options selected).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Microsoft has implemented a variety of security support providers for use with RPC sessions. All of the options must be enabled to ensure the maximum security level.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253466 · WN11-SO-000230 · CAT II: The system must be configured to use FIPS-compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253466r1210303_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000478-GPOS-00223 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140), File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-002450 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-13 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-13 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The system must be configured to use FIPS-compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.
- *Group Policy*: The central way Windows administrators push settings to many computers at once.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\PolicyManager\current\device\Cryptography!AllowFipsAlgorithmPolicy_ProviderSet  (For Intune-managed systems) | Enabled | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, 'System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing' (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\FIPSAlgorithmPolicy\Enabled) restricts Schannel and CNG to FIPS-approved algorithms. Related settings cover Kerberos encryption types and NTLM session security.

**Also related (File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access):** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java and .NET code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\FIPSAlgorithmPolicy\  (For GPO-managed systems)
Or
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\PolicyManager\current\device\Cryptography!AllowFipsAlgorithmPolicy_ProviderSet  (For Intune-managed systems)

Value Name: Enabled

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1

Warning: Clients with this setting enabled will not be able to communicate via digitally encrypted or signed protocols with servers that do not support these algorithms.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
For GPO-managed systems:

Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing" to "Enabled".

For Intune-managed systems:

Set the Intune System Cryptography Policy to use FIPS-compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** This setting ensures the system uses algorithms that are FIPS compliant for encryption, hashing, and signing. FIPS-compliant algorithms meet specific standards established by the U.S. Government and must be the algorithms used for all OS encryption functions.

Note: A different registry location is needed when systems are managed by Intune versus GPO.

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002450**: Implement organization-defined types of cryptography for each specified cryptography use.  
  Rev 5: SC-13 b · Rev 4: SC-13 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253467 · WN11-SO-000240 · CAT III: The default permissions of global system objects must be increased.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253467r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The default permissions of global system objects must be increased.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager | ProtectionMode | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | System objects: Strengthen default permissions of internal system objects (e.g. Symbolic links) | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\

Value Name: ProtectionMode

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "System objects: Strengthen default permissions of internal system objects (e.g. Symbolic links)" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Windows systems maintain a global list of shared system resources such as DOS device names, mutexes, and semaphores. Each type of object is created with a default DACL that specifies who can access the objects with what permissions. If this policy is enabled, the default DACL is stronger, allowing non-admin users to read shared objects, but not modify shared objects that they did not create.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253468 · WN11-SO-000245 · CAT II: User Account Control approval mode for the built-in Administrator must be enabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253468r1051057_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000373-GPOS-00157 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening, Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo) |
| CCI | CCI-002038 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-11 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-11 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** User Account Control approval mode for the built-in Administrator must be enabled.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *UAC*: User Account Control: the Windows pop-up that asks for confirmation before something makes system-wide changes.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System | FilterAdministratorToken | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | User Account Control: Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows these are Security Options ('Accounts: Rename administrator account', 'Accounts: Guest account status', 'Accounts: Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only') plus LAPS for unique, rotated local administrator passwords.

**Also related (Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo)):** UAC settings are Security Options named 'User Account Control: ...' (registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System: EnableLUA, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin, ConsentPromptBehaviorUser, FilterAdministratorToken, EnableInstallerDetection, EnableSecureUIAPaths, EnableVirtualization).

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\

Value Name: FilterAdministratorToken

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "User Account Control: Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** User Account Control (UAC) is a security mechanism for limiting the elevation of privileges, including administrative accounts, unless authorized. This setting configures the built-in Administrator account so that it runs in Admin Approval Mode.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002038**: The organization requires users to reauthenticate upon organization-defined circumstances or situations requiring reauthentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-11 · Rev 4: IA-11 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253469 · WN11-SO-000250 · CAT II: User Account Control must prompt administrators for consent on the secure desktop.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253469r958518_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000134-GPOS-00068 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo) |
| CCI | CCI-001084 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** User Account Control must prompt administrators for consent on the secure desktop.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *UAC*: User Account Control: the Windows pop-up that asks for confirmation before something makes system-wide changes.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System | ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin | REG_DWORD = 2 (Prompt for consent on the secure desktop) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators in Admin Approval Mode | "Prompt for consent on the secure desktop" |

**How it works:** UAC settings are Security Options named 'User Account Control: ...' (registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System: EnableLUA, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin, ConsentPromptBehaviorUser, FilterAdministratorToken, EnableInstallerDetection, EnableSecureUIAPaths, EnableVirtualization).

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\

Value Name: ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 2 (Prompt for consent on the secure desktop)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators in Admin Approval Mode" to "Prompt for consent on the secure desktop".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** User Account Control (UAC) is a security mechanism for limiting the elevation of privileges, including administrative accounts, unless authorized. This setting configures the elevation requirements for logged on administrators to complete a task that requires raised privileges.

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001084**: Isolate security functions from nonsecurity functions.  
  Rev 5: SC-3 · Rev 4: SC-3 · Rev 3: SC-3

### V-253470 · WN11-SO-000251 · CAT II: Windows 11 must use multifactor authentication for local and network access to privileged and nonprivileged accounts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253470r1268228_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000105-GPOS-00052 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000765 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-2 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-2 (1) |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must use multifactor authentication for local and network access to privileged and nonprivileged accounts.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the system is not a member of a domain, this is Not Applicable.

If all of the following settings exist and are populated, this is not a finding.

\HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\Calais\Readers
\HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\Calais\SmartCards
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
For nondomain joined systems, configuring Windows Hello for sign-on options would be suggested based on the organization's needs and capabilities.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the use of multifactor authentication, the ease of access to privileged and nonprivileged functions is greatly increased.

All domain accounts must be enabled for multifactor authentication with the exception of local emergency accounts.

Multifactor authentication requires using two or more factors to achieve authentication.

Factors include:

1) Something a user knows (e.g., password/PIN);

2) Something a user has (e.g., cryptographic identification device, token); and

3) Something a user is (e.g., biometric).

A privileged account is defined as an information system account with authorizations of a privileged user.

Network access is defined as access to an information system by a user (or a process acting on behalf of a user) communicating through a network (e.g., local area network, wide area network, or the internet).

Local access is defined as access to an organizational information system by a user (or process acting on behalf of a user) communicating through a direct connection without the use of a network.

The DoW CAC with DoW-approved PKI is an example of multifactor authentication.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000106-GPOS-00053, SRG-OS-000107-GPOS-00054, SRG-OS-000108-GPOS-00055

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000765**: Implement multifactor authentication for access to privileged accounts.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (1) · Rev 4: IA-2 (1) · Rev 3: IA-2 (1)

**In plain terms:** User Account Control must be configured to detect application installations and prompt for elevation.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *UAC*: User Account Control: the Windows pop-up that asks for confirmation before something makes system-wide changes.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System | EnableInstallerDetection | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | User Account Control: Detect application installations and prompt for elevation | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** UAC settings are Security Options named 'User Account Control: ...' (registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System: EnableLUA, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin, ConsentPromptBehaviorUser, FilterAdministratorToken, EnableInstallerDetection, EnableSecureUIAPaths, EnableVirtualization).

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\

Value Name: EnableInstallerDetection

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> "User Account Control: Detect application installations and prompt for elevation" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** User Account Control (UAC) is a security mechanism for limiting the elevation of privileges, including administrative accounts, unless authorized. This setting requires Windows to respond to application installation requests by prompting for credentials.

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001084**: Isolate security functions from nonsecurity functions.  
  Rev 5: SC-3 · Rev 4: SC-3 · Rev 3: SC-3

### V-253476 · WN11-SO-000280 · CAT II: Passwords for enabled local Administrator accounts must be changed at least every 180 days.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253476r1268211_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000076-GPOS-00044 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse, Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-004066, CCI-000199 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Passwords for enabled local Administrator accounts must be changed at least every 180 days.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy: 'Maximum password age', 'Minimum password age', 'Enforce password history'. Domain values come from the Default Domain Policy or PSOs.

**Also related (Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening):** On Windows these are Security Options ('Accounts: Rename administrator account', 'Accounts: Guest account status', 'Accounts: Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only') plus LAPS for unique, rotated local administrator passwords.

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If there are no enabled local Administrator accounts, this is Not Applicable.

Use of an enabled built-in account without management by LAPS must be documented and supplied to the information system security manager (ISSM)/information system security officer (ISSO) for their risk acceptance.

An alternative process to LAPS is acceptable if it is documented and produces evidence that passwords for Administrator accounts are changed at least every 180 days.

Review the password last set date for the enabled local Administrator account.

On the standalone or domain-joined workstation:

Open "PowerShell".

Enter "Get-LocalUser -Name * | Select-Object *".

If the "PasswordLastSet" date is greater than "180" days old for the local Administrator account for administering the computer/domain, this is a finding.

Verify LAPS is configured and operational.

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> LAPS >> Password Settings >> Set to enabled. Password Complexity, large letters + small letters + numbers + special, Password Length 14, Password Age 180. If not configured as shown, this is a finding.

Verify LAPS Operational logs >> Event Viewer >> Applications and Services Logs >> Microsoft >> Windows >> LAPS >> Operational. Verify LAPS policy process is completing. If it is not, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Change the enabled local Administrator account password at least every 180 days.

Windows LAPS must be used to change the built-in Administrator account password. Domain-joined and nondomain-joined systems can configure this to occur more frequently. LAPS will change the password every 30 days by default.

Operational limitations preventing the use of LAPS must be approved by the AO.

More information is available at:
https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/windows-it-pro-blog/by-popular-demand-windows-laps-available-now/ba-p/3788747
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-overview#windows-laps-supported-platforms-and-azure-ad-laps-preview-status
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The longer a password is in use, the greater the opportunity for someone to gain unauthorized knowledge of the password. A local Administrator account is not generally used and its password may not be changed as frequently as necessary. Changing the password for enabled Administrator accounts on a regular basis will limit their exposure.

Windows LAPS must be used to change the built-in Administrator account password. Operational limitations preventing the use of Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) must be approved by the authorizing official (AO).

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing; T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000199**: The information system enforces maximum password lifetime restrictions.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (d)
