### V-253477 · WN11-UC-000015 · CAT III: Toast notifications to the lock screen must be turned off.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253477r1260004_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout, Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Toast notifications to the lock screen must be turned off.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\PushNotifications | NoToastApplicationNotificationOnLockScreen | REG_DWORD = 1 |
| Group Policy | User Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Start Menu and Taskbar >> Notifications | Turn off toast notifications on the lock screen | "Enabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows, set 'Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit' (InactivityTimeoutSecs <= 900) and 'Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior' (Lock Workstation). Personalization policies prevent the lock screen from showing slide shows or camera access.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On Windows, use Security Options such as 'Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in' and 'Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL' (Disabled). Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon covers enumerating local users, convenience PIN and picture password. Credential User Interface >> 'Do not display the password reveal button' handles the reveal button.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This Check must be performed for each interactive user profile on the system.
If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_CURRENT_USER
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\PushNotifications\

Value Name: NoToastApplicationNotificationOnLockScreen

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 1

Note: This requirement is applicable to profiles for interactive logins. It is not applicable for Service accounts.

To determine the system's enabled user profiles:
Run "PowerShell" as an administrator.

Execute the following command:
Get-LocalUser | Where-Object {$_.Enabled -eq $true}
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
For each user profile on the system, configure the policy value for User Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Start Menu and Taskbar >> Notifications >> "Turn off toast notifications on the lock screen" to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Toast notifications that are displayed on the lock screen could display sensitive information to unauthorized personnel. Turning off this feature will limit access to the information to a logged on user.

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1087 Account Discovery

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-253478 · WN11-UC-000020 · CAT II: Zone information must be preserved when saving attachments.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253478r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Zone information must be preserved when saving attachments.

**Why it matters:** Modern computers like to "phone home", sending usage data to the manufacturer, syncing to personal cloud accounts, or showing ads and suggestions. This rule turns those features off or down so government information stays inside the government's systems, like not letting a delivery driver wander through the office and take notes.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Attachments | SaveZoneInformation | REG_DWORD = 0x00000002 (2) (or if the Value Name does not exist) |
| Group Policy | User Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Attachment Manager | Do not preserve zone information in file attachments | "Not Configured" or "Disabled" |

**How it works:** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Users lose consumer conveniences such as Store apps, Microsoft-account sign-in and web results in search. Enterprise management may need a minimum telemetry level (e.g. for Windows Update for Business reports), so align the value with the STIG's allowed options.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This Check must be performed for each interactive user profile on the system.

The default behavior is for Windows to mark file attachments with their zone information.

If it exists and is configured with a value of "1", this is a finding.

Registry Hive: HKEY_CURRENT_USER
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Attachments\

Value Name: SaveZoneInformation

Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000002 (2) (or if the Value Name does not exist)

Note: This requirement is applicable to profiles for interactive logins. It is not applicable for Service accounts.

To determine the system's enabled user profiles:
Run "PowerShell" as an administrator.

Execute the following command:
Get-LocalUser | Where-Object {$_.Enabled -eq $true}
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
The default behavior is for Windows to mark file attachments with their zone information.

To correct this, (for each user profile on the system) configure the policy value for User Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Attachment Manager >> "Do not preserve zone information in file attachments" to "Not Configured" or "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Preserving zone of origin (internet, intranet, local, restricted) information on file attachments allows Windows to determine risk.

**Threat & control context:** Consumer-oriented and cloud-connected features can move government data (documents, typed input, location, diagnostic dumps containing memory contents) to vendor or third-party services outside the authorization boundary. Disabling or restricting them supports SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-20 (use of external systems), CM-7 and privacy controls, and removes unvetted functionality from the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-253479 · WN11-UR-000005 · CAT II: The "Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller" user right must not be assigned to any groups or accounts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253479r958726_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment, Credential Storage & Password Hashing |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The "Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller" user right must not be assigned to any groups or accounts.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller | No accounts or groups (defined, blank) |

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Credential Storage & Password Hashing):** Relevant Windows settings include 'Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' (NoLMHash), 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' (Disabled), and 'Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache' (CachedLogonsCount).

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any groups or accounts are granted the "Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller" user right, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> "Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller" to be defined but containing no entries (blank).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller" user right may be able to retrieve the credentials of other accounts from Credential Manager.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253480 · WN11-UR-000010 · CAT II: The "Access this computer from the network" user right must only be assigned to the Administrators and Remote Desktop Users groups.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253480r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment, Remote Desktop & Remote Management |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The "Access this computer from the network" user right must only be assigned to the Administrators and Remote Desktop Users groups.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Remote Desktop (RDP)*: A way to see and control a Windows computer's screen from another computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Access this computer from the network | Only: Administrators, Remote Desktop Users |

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Remote Desktop & Remote Management):** On Windows, RDP settings are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Remote Desktop Services >> Remote Desktop Session Host (Security / Device and Resource Redirection / Session Time Limits), and WinRM settings under Windows Components >> Windows Remote Management (WinRM Client / WinRM Service). Verify WinRM with 'winrm get winrm/config'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any groups or accounts other than the following are granted the "Access this computer from the network" user right, this is a finding:

Administrators
Remote Desktop Users

If a domain application account such as for a management tool requires this user right, this would not be a finding.

Vendor documentation must support the requirement for having the user right.

The requirement must be documented with the ISSO.

The application account, managed at the domain level, must meet requirements for application account passwords, such as length and frequency of changes as defined in the Windows Server STIGs.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> "Access this computer from the network" to only include the following groups or accounts:

Administrators
Remote Desktop Users
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Access this computer from the network" user right may access resources on the system, and must be limited to those that require it.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

Accounts with the "Create a pagefile" user right can change the size of a pagefile, which could affect system performance.

Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The "Create a token object" user right must not be assigned to any groups or accounts.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Create a token object | No accounts or groups (defined, blank) |

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication):** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any groups or accounts are granted the "Create a token object" user right, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> "Create a token object" to be defined but containing no entries (blank).
```

### V-253491 · WN11-UR-000070 · CAT II: The "Deny access to this computer from the network" user right on workstations must be configured to prevent access from highly privileged domain accounts and local accounts on domain systems and unauthenticated access on all systems.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253491r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment, Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The "Deny access to this computer from the network" user right on workstations must be configured to prevent access from highly privileged domain accounts and local accounts on domain systems and unauthenticated access on all systems.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Deny access | Only: Enterprise Admins group, Domain Admins group, Local account (see Note below) |

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Account Lifecycle Management):** On Windows, use 'Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 35' for domain accounts. For local accounts, review 'Get-LocalUser' (LastLogon, PasswordExpires) and disable or delete accounts that aren't needed. Shared accounts require ISSO-documented justification.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If the following groups or accounts are not defined for the "Deny access to this computer from the network" right, this is a finding:

Domain Systems Only:
Enterprise Admins group
Domain Admins group
Local account (see Note below)

All Systems:
Guests group

Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) dedicated to the management of Active Directory are exempt from denying the Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins groups. (See the Windows Privileged Access Workstation STIG for PAW requirements.)

Note: "Local account" is a built-in security group used to assign user rights and permissions to all local accounts.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> "Deny access to this computer from the network" to include the following:

Domain Systems Only:
Enterprise Admins group
Domain Admins group
Local account (see Note below)

All Systems:
Guests group

Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) dedicated to the management of Active Directory are exempt from denying the Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins groups. (See the Windows Privileged Access Workstation STIG for PAW requirements.)

Note: "Local account" is a built-in security group used to assign user rights and permissions to all local accounts.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

The "Deny access to this computer from the network" right defines the accounts that are prevented from logging on from the network.

In an Active Directory Domain, denying logons to the Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins groups on lower trust systems helps mitigate the risk of privilege escalation from credential theft attacks, which could lead to the compromise of an entire domain.

Local accounts on domain-joined systems must also be assigned this right to decrease the risk of lateral movement resulting from credential theft attacks.

The Guests group must be assigned this right to prevent unauthenticated access.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Deny log on as a batch job | Only: Enterprise Admin Group, Domain Admin Group |

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Active Directory & Domain Controller Security):** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

```text
If the following groups or accounts are not defined for the "Deny log on as a batch job" right, this is a finding:

Domain Systems Only:
Enterprise Admin Group
Domain Admin Group
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text

Enterprise Admin Group
Domain Admin Group
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

The "Deny log on as a batch job" right defines accounts that are prevented from logging on to the system as a batch job, such as Task Scheduler.

In an Active Directory Domain, denying logons to the Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins groups on lower trust systems helps mitigate the risk of privilege escalation from credential theft attacks which could lead to the compromise of an entire domain.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The "Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services" user right on this computer workstations must be configured to prevent access from highly privileged domain accounts and local accounts on domain systems and unauthenticated access on all systems.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *Remote Desktop (RDP)*: A way to see and control a Windows computer's screen from another computer.
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services | include the following |

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Account Lifecycle Management):** On Windows, use 'Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 35' for domain accounts. For local accounts, review 'Get-LocalUser' (LastLogon, PasswordExpires) and disable or delete accounts that aren't needed. Shared accounts require ISSO-documented justification.

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

All Systems:
Guests group
```

```text
Domain Systems Only:
Enterprise Admins group
Domain Admins group
Local account (see Note below)

All Systems:
Guests group

Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) dedicated to the management of Active Directory are exempt from denying the Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins groups. (See the Windows Privileged Access Workstation STIG for PAW requirements.)

Note: "Local account" is a built-in security group used to assign user rights and permissions to all local accounts.
```

In an Active Directory Domain, denying logons to the Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins groups on lower trust systems helps mitigate the risk of privilege escalation from credential theft attacks, which could lead to the compromise of an entire domain.

Local accounts on domain-joined systems must also be assigned this right to decrease the risk of lateral movement resulting from credential theft attacks.

The Guests group must be assigned this right to prevent unauthenticated access.

Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-253498 · WN11-UR-000110 · CAT II: The "Impersonate a client after authentication" user right must only be assigned to Administrators, Service, Local Service, and Network Service.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253498r1138526_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The "Impersonate a client after authentication" user right must only be assigned to Administrators, Service, Local Service, and Network Service.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Impersonate a client after authentication | Only: Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, RESTRICTED SERVICES\PrintSpoolerService, SERVICE |

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any groups or accounts other than the following are granted the "Impersonate a client after authentication" user right, this is a finding:

Administrators
LOCAL SERVICE
NETWORK SERVICE
RESTRICTED SERVICES\PrintSpoolerService
SERVICE
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> "Impersonate a client after authentication" to only include the following groups or accounts:

Administrators
LOCAL SERVICE
NETWORK SERVICE
RESTRICTED SERVICES\PrintSpoolerService
SERVICE
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

The "Impersonate a client after authentication" user right allows a program to impersonate another user or account to run on their behalf. An attacker could potentially use this to elevate privileges.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> "Profile single process" to only include the following groups or accounts:

Administrators
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Profile single process" user right can monitor non-system processes performance. An attacker could potentially use this to identify processes to attack.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-253505 · WN11-UR-000160 · CAT II: The "Restore files and directories" user right must only be assigned to the Administrators group.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-253505r958726_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment, Backup & Recovery |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The "Restore files and directories" user right must only be assigned to the Administrators group.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Restore files and directories | Only: Administrators |

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Backup & Recovery):** On Windows, review the backup tooling and the 'Back up files and directories' and 'Restore files and directories' user rights (Administrators only). Protect the directory services restore mode (DSRM) password on DCs and the system state backups.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any groups or accounts other than the following are granted the "Restore files and directories" user right, this is a finding:

Administrators
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> "Restore files and directories" to only include the following groups or accounts:

Administrators
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Restore files and directories" user right can circumvent file and directory permissions and could allow access to sensitive data. It could also be used to over-write more current data.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1490 Inhibit System Recovery; T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a
